Option 2 reverses the direction (subcritical to supercritical), which would contradict the stated premise that networks are inherently supercritical and that clustering moves them toward criticality. So Option 1's findings better support the authors' idea.

The authors' hypothesis is that increasing clustering tunes networks from supercritical toward critical (mesoscale criticality) dynamics. Option 1 reports a transition from subcritical to supercritical with increasing clustering, which does not match the proposed direction of tuning inherently supercritical networks toward criticality; Option 2 reports a transition from supercritical to subcritical, which is the direction the authors predict, with moderately clustered networks showing power-law avalanches. Option 2 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

The two abstracts are identical except for the comparative findings. Option 1 reports SA-I responses to static torque as inferior to dynamic stimuli in humans and discrimination capacity as inferior in humans than monkeys. Option 2 reports the opposite: superior static responses and superior discrimination in humans. The authors' idea is that human tactile afferents encode torque and that differences from monkeys reflect tissue compliance and friction. Both versions support encoding, but Option 2's findings, with humans showing superior discrimination and static encoding, make the compensatory account via SA-II input and human-specific mechanisms look more strongly supported as a distinct, advantageous human capacity. Option 1 frames humans as needing compensation, which is a weaker, more hedged picture. Option 2 therefore favours the authors' idea more.

The two abstracts differ only in the comparative findings. Option 1 reports SA-I responses to static torque were superior to dynamic in humans and that discrimination capacity was superior in humans than monkeys, framing human afferents as more capable. Option 2 reports the opposite: inferior static responses and inferior discrimination in humans. The authors' idea is that human tactile afferents encode torque well and that SA-II input compensates; Option 1's findings present human encoding as superior, which better supports that idea than Option 2's inferior framing.

Both abstracts are nearly identical; the only differences are that Option 1 reports two potential sodium-binding sites and places the MD sodium ions at the E373 position, while Option 2 reports three sites and places them at the M335A position. Option 1's version is internally consistent with the abstract's own emphasis on E373 as a sodium-sensitive site (E373 mutants abolish sodium sensitivity, and the two-site count matches the two sites concluded: E373 and D863/E865 pocket). Option 2 is internally inconsistent: it claims three sites but concludes with only two sodium-sensitive sites, and locates sodium at a mutant residue rather than a native site. Option 1 therefore presents the authors' proposed sodium-binding mechanism more coherently and supportively, so it favours the authors' idea somewhat more.

Both abstracts report the same study design, mutant screen, and conclusions. The only difference is the count of sodium-binding sites (three in Option 1 versus two in Option 2) and where MD sodium ions sit (M335A position in Option 1 versus E373 position in Option 2). The authors' idea is a set of sodium-sensitive sites in the Slack C-terminus, identified by mutagenesis and MD. Option 1's finding of three potential sites, including one at the M335A position supported by MD, offers a somewhat richer set of supported candidates, while Option 2's internally consistent E373-based MD account is tighter. Neither clearly favours the authors' idea more, so the probability is near even, with a slight tilt toward Option 1 for its broader identification of sites.

The authors hypothesize that replay recruitment incorporates new contextual information into a previously stabilized spatial representation. Option 1 reports that remapping cells, which reflect new contextual learning, are recruited into replay more than stable cells, directly supporting that the new information is being incorporated via replay. Option 2 reports the reverse, with stable cells recruited more, which would instead suggest replay mainly reinforces the existing stabilized representation and fits the hypothesis less well. Option 1 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

The authors' idea is that replay recruitment incorporates new contextual information into a stabilized spatial representation. Option 1 reports that stable cells, which keep their spatial representation, are recruited into replay more, which fits a model where replay consolidates an established map while new information is folded in via stable cells. Option 2 reports that remapping cells (the ones encoding new task context) are recruited more, which more directly supports the claim that replay incorporates new contextual information. Option 2 therefore better matches the authors' stated interpretation.

The authors hypothesize that withdrawal disrupts emotional learning circuits via reduced endogenous peptide control of neurotransmission. Option 1 reports that withdrawal reduces peptide inhibition of BLA-ITC transmission, which directly supports the hypothesized disruption and the proposed remedy of restoring peptide activity. Option 2 reports increased peptide inhibition, which contradicts the framing of withdrawal as disrupting circuits and undermines their proposed mechanism. Option 1's findings therefore favour the authors' idea more clearly.

The authors hypothesized that withdrawal disrupts amygdala circuits by altering endogenous opioid peptide control of BLA-ITC transmission. Option 2 reports that withdrawal reduces peptide inhibition, which fits a model where withdrawal weakens endogenous peptide control and shifts excitatory/inhibitory balance, consistent with the proposed mechanism and the restoration-of-peptide-activity rationale. Option 1 reports increased peptide inhibition, which is less coherent with the stated disruption narrative and the proposed PKA-driven peptidase increase framing (peptidase upregulation would be expected to reduce peptide activity). The authors' idea is better supported by Option 2's findings.

The authors' idea is that longitudinal changes in specific LPFC sulcal morphology are behaviorally meaningful and predict reasoning development. Option 1 reports that cortical thickness of four left-hemisphere sulci predicts reasoning change, showing a broader set of sulci with a clear structural-behavioral link. Option 2 reports only two right-hemisphere sulci with surface area changes, a narrower and less robust link. Option 1 therefore appears to support the authors' claim more strongly.

The authors' idea is that longitudinal changes in specific LPFC sulcal morphology are behaviorally meaningful for reasoning development. Option 1 reports surface area changes in two right-hemisphere sulci predicting reasoning changes, with surface area being the morphological measure that showed both cross-sectional and longitudinal developmental effects. Option 2 reports cortical thickness changes in four left-hemisphere sulci predicting reasoning, but cortical thickness is not described as showing longitudinal change in a way that supports the sulcal-flattening framing as strongly, and the predictor set is larger and less specific. Option 1's findings more coherently link developmental morphology change to cognition, so they favour the authors' idea more.

The authors' idea is that prefrontal cortex is central to cognitive control, so PFC should lead and dominate contextual representations. Option 1 says cue responses appear first in parietal cortex but are stronger and more persistent in PFC, and that control demand biases context toward PFC. This supports the PFC-centric framing. Option 2 reverses these, placing context dominance in parietal cortex, which undercuts the authors' PFC emphasis. Option 1 therefore better favours the authors' idea.

The study's idea is that prefrontal cortex mediates cognitive control, so findings showing PFC carries stronger, more persistent contextual information and that control demand biases context representation toward PFC would favour that idea. Option 2 says this (stronger, persistent context in PFC; bias toward PFC), whereas Option 1 assigns these properties to parietal cortex, undermining the PFC-centred account. Option 2 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

Both abstracts support the evoked-response idea equally in their conclusions, but Option 1 reports theta-and-delta phase-locking for slow speech, which fits the evoked-response model's predicted low-frequency transient responses, while Option 2 reports theta-and-alpha for fast speech, a different and less directly predicted pattern. The authors' evoked-response hypothesis is therefore slightly better supported by Option 1's specific findings, though the difference is modest.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis contest (oscillatory entrainment vs. evoked responses) and the authors favour the evoked-response account. Option 1 reports theta and alpha phase-locking for fast speech, which the evoked model explains but entrainment does not; Option 2 reports theta and delta phase-locking for slow speech, a finding that is equally compatible with evoked responses. The only difference is the speech-rate condition and frequency band. Option 1's finding is somewhat more discriminating because alpha activity is less expected from entrainment of low-frequency envelope oscillations, giving it a slight edge for the authors' idea, but the difference is modest.

The two abstracts differ in their supporting findings. Option 1 reports that superior R neurons encode the motion-defined bar, that the luminance-defined bar evokes consistent excitation in superior bulb R neurons while inferior bulb shows mixed responses (a clear contrast supporting functional subdivision), and that R4d neurons specifically are vital. Option 2 reports consistent inhibition in superior bulb R neurons, and a less clearly contrasting comparison ('either excited or inhibited responses in the superior bulb' rather than inferior), which weakens the claimed functional division. Option 2 also shifts the key behavioral role to TuBu neurons, which is less directly tied to the R-neuron-centred hypothesis. Option 1's findings more cleanly support the authors' idea of a distinct superior R-neuron pathway encoding motion-defined features.

The two abstracts differ in three places: Option 1 reports consistent inhibition of superior R neurons to the luminance bar and excited or inhibited responses in the superior bulb, and attributes the behavioral role to TuBu neurons. Option 2 reports consistent excitation in superior R neurons and excited or inhibited responses in the inferior bulb, and attributes the role to R4d neurons. The authors' central idea is that superior R/TuBu circuitry encodes motion-defined features and that bulb subdomains are functionally divided. Option 1 supports this more directly: its superior-bulb results show a distinct response pattern separating the two bar types within the superior domain, and its behavioral conclusion points to the superior TuBu pathway the authors emphasize. Option 2 locates the functional contrast in the inferior bulb and names a different cell type, which weakens the superior-pathway story. Option 1 is therefore modestly more favourable to the authors' idea.

The authors' idea is partial recovery of anticipatory control through neuroplastic changes. Option 1 reports complete clearance increasing over time, paralleling recovery of muscle activation patterns, which supports recovery of anticipatory control. Option 2 reports complete clearance decreasing and diverging from muscle activation recovery, which undermines the claim of recovery. Option 1 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

The authors' idea is that locomotor recovery after hemisection reflects partial recovery of anticipatory control through neuroplasticity, which is best supported when obstacle clearance improves over time. Option 2 reports that complete clearance increased from weeks 1-2 to 7-8, with Other responses decreasing and the increase paralleling recovery of muscle activation patterns. Option 1 reports the opposite: clearance decreased and diverged from recovery. Option 2's findings therefore align more closely with the authors' recovery-based interpretation, so Option 1's findings favour the idea far less.

The authors' idea is that dopamine loss alters Mthal-driven activation of M1 in a specific, mechanistic way. Option 1 reports laminar-specific changes in intracortical transmission and frequency-dependent synaptic dynamics, which give a more precise and detailed circuit account than Option 2's cell-type-specific changes and frequency-independent dynamics. The more specific, detailed findings in Option 1 better support a circuit-level mechanism, so they likely please the authors more.

The authors' idea is that dopamine loss alters Mthal-to-M1 activation in a specific, circuit-level way. Option 1 reports changes that are cell type-specific in intracortical transmission and frequency-independent in synaptic dynamics, which is a more specific and arguably less diffuse claim. Option 2 reports laminar-specific changes and frequency-dependent dynamics, which map onto the framing of laminar circuit mechanisms. Both support the same conclusion; the difference is modest, and neither clearly favours the authors' idea more.

The two abstracts are identical except for which mPFC subregion is linked to which finding (ventral/rostral/dorsal in Option 1 versus dorsal/caudal/ventral in Option 2). Neither version's behavioral or overall conclusions differ, and the hierarchical allostatic regulation model is supported equally by both mappings. Since the authors' idea (the hierarchical allostatic model with distinct subregional roles) is supported regardless of which label goes where, neither version clearly favours the authors' idea more.

The two abstracts are identical except for which mPFC subregion is linked to which effect. Neither version's findings are inherently more supportive of the authors' hierarchical allostatic regulation model; both assert the same model support and conclusion, differing only in regional labels. Thus neither favours the authors' idea over the other.

The authors' idea is that a functional brain marker of delay discounting is a meaningful, generalizable biomarker linked to obesity and metabolism. Option 2 reports that discounting behavior itself also differed between overweight and lean individuals, which adds a behavioral correlate and broadens support for the link to obesity. Option 1 specifically notes that the brain marker, but not behavior, differed by weight status. The marker-specific finding in Option 1 is the stronger demonstration of the brain marker's added value, which is the authors' central claim, so Option 1 better favours the authors' idea of a distinctive brain marker, though the difference is modest.

The authors' idea is that the fMRI functional brain marker generalizes and tracks obesity-related differences. Option 1 reports that both the brain marker and discounting behavior differ significantly between overweight and lean individuals, which supports the broader claim that delay discounting is linked to obesity and that the marker captures this. Option 2 reports that only the brain marker differs, not behavior. This still supports the marker idea, but the lack of a behavioral difference weakens the link between discounting and obesity that the paper emphasizes. Option 1's findings therefore favour the authors' idea more.

The authors' idea is that phasic taVNS activates the LC-NA system and that pupillary light reflex serves as a taVNS biomarker. Option 1 reports taVNS increasing pupil dilation and performance, increasing frontal-midline theta/alpha, and reducing occipital alpha, which matches the expected LC-NA activation pattern and supports the proposed biomarkers. Option 2 reports decreased dilation and performance, decreased theta/alpha, and increased occipital alpha, which would argue against LC-NA activation. Option 1's findings therefore better favour the authors' hypothesis.

The authors' idea is that phasic taVNS modulates LC-NA biomarkers and that the pupillary light reflex is an effective taVNS proxy. Option 1 reports decreased pupil dilation, reduced performance, decreased frontal theta/alpha, increased occipital alpha, and reduced/delayed dilation in the PLRT. Option 2 reports increased dilation and performance, increased frontal theta/alpha, reduced occipital alpha, and reduced/delayed constriction. Both versions claim systematic modulation, so the study's core claim holds in each. Option 2's findings align more with the LC-NA activation hypothesis (noradrenergic activation typically increases pupil dilation and frontal theta), giving the authors' framing of activation a cleaner fit. Option 1's decreases are harder to interpret as LC-NA activation, though they still show modulation. Overall Option 2 better supports the authors' idea.

The authors' idea is that theta-frequency inputs to IL drive synaptic changes that suppress fear memories, with theta (especially 4 Hz) being specifically effective. Option 1 states that inputs at other frequencies were ineffective and did not suppress fear memories, which directly supports the frequency-specificity claim central to the hypothesis. Option 2 states other frequencies were also effective, which undermines the specificity of the theta-band mechanism. Hence Option 1's findings favour the authors' idea more.

The authors' idea is that theta-frequency inputs to IL drive fear suppression via synaptic changes. Option 1 reports that inputs at other frequencies were also effective, broadening the mechanism and showing the effect is not restricted to theta, which is a weaker, less specific claim. Option 2 reports that other frequencies were ineffective, so the theta-specific account is sharply supported and the contrast with non-theta inputs gives a clearer validation of the hypothesis. The authors would therefore be more pleased with Option 2's findings.

The authors' idea is that DCN UBCs rely on mGluR1 and show a continuum of response durations rather than distinct excitatory and inhibitory subtypes. Both options share this conclusion and the mGluR1 result, so the difference lies only in the specific durations described. Option 1 reports a range from 100 ms excitation to seconds-long excitation-to-inhibition sequences, which better captures a graded continuum of durations spanning fast to slow responses. Option 2 describes a narrower spread (500 ms to 100 ms, lasting several seconds), which fits the continuum claim less cleanly. Option 1 therefore supports the authors' hypothesis slightly more, though the difference is modest.

The authors' idea is that DCN UBCs rely on mGluR1 and show a continuum of response durations rather than distinct excitatory/inhibitory subtypes. Option 1 reports a continuum spanning 500 ms excitation to prolonged inhibition, a range that is broad and consistent with the proposed graded continuum, and its excitatory responses are mGluR1-mediated, supporting the mGluR1 claim. Option 2 reports 100 ms excitation to several seconds of excitation then inhibition lasting hundreds of milliseconds; the mixed, shorter-scale profile is similarly continuous but the response durations appear less extended and less clearly graded. Both share the same mGluR1 conclusion, so the difference lies mainly in how cleanly the continuum is depicted. Option 1 presents a somewhat more coherent continuum with mGluR1-dominant excitation, so it likely favours the authors' idea modestly more.

The authors' idea is that FFI timing in the cerebellum is complex and that MF stimulation recruits varied GC groups producing a wide range of E/I delays, expanding PC temporal integration, which would make the temporal-organization hypothesis look more strongly supported. Option 1 reports wide delays from MF stimulation, low variability with direct GC stimulation, and a strong influence of temporal expansion on PC integration, which fits that claim. Option 2 reports narrow delays, high variability with direct GC stimulation, no expansion, and only a moderate influence, which weakens the hypothesis. Option 1 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

The authors' idea is that the cerebellar FFI pathway has a temporally organized, variable E/I delay structure that helps Purkinje cells encode specific mossy fiber inputs. Option 1 reports a narrow range of E delays and a high variability only under direct GC stimulation, with temporal expansion only moderately influencing integration. Option 2 reports a wide range of delays through MF stimulation and temporal expansion that strongly influences PC integration, which more directly supports the claim that specific E/I delays shape PC encoding. Option 2 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

The authors' idea is that a delayed GABA shift (kept depolarizing by KCC2 inhibition) has consequences for network development. Option 1 reports that depolarizing GABA does not promote synapse formation after P7 and that structural/functional development is unaffected, which weakens a view that the delayed shift matters structurally. Option 2 reports that depolarizing GABA promotes synapse formation and that excitatory development is affected, while inhibitory synapses are not, supporting a clear causal effect of the delayed shift. Since the study set out to show an impact of the delayed shift, Option 2's findings better support the authors' idea.

The authors' idea is that a delayed GABA shift (kept depolarizing via KCC2 inhibition) affects network development and that depolarizing GABA promotes synapse formation after P7. Option 1 reports that excitatory synapse development at DIV9 was affected and that depolarizing GABA signaling promotes synapse formation, directly supporting that hypothesis. Option 2 reports no effect on synapse development and that depolarizing GABA does not promote synapse formation, contradicting it. Option 1 therefore favours the authors' idea more clearly.

Option 1 reports that predicted contents flexibly propagate depending on task demands, under prefrontal supervisory control, and that predictions enhance both LSF and HSF bottom-up representations leading to faster categorization. This gives a richer, more mechanistic and behaviorally consequential account that fits the authors' prediction-facilitates-categorization hypothesis. Option 2 reports content propagation irrespective of task demands, control by premotor rather than prefrontal cortex, an LSF-only enhancement, and limited behavioral effect, all of which weaken the authors' idea. Option 1 therefore favours the authors' idea more clearly.

Both abstracts describe the same study, but Option 2 reports findings that more directly support the authors' hypothesis that predictions facilitate categorization: predicted contents flexibly propagate depending on task demands, predictions enhance LSF versus HSF representations, and this produces faster categorization behavior. Option 1 reports that task demands do not affect propagation and that the effect on categorization behavior is limited, which weakens the authors' proposed mechanism. Option 2's findings therefore favour the authors' idea more.

The authors' idea is that the 3D structural architecture of the human hand area is nontopographic, which they support by finding no structural differences, no low-myelin borders, and high similarity between fingers. Option 1 reports an absence of differences, an absence of borders, and high similarity, which fits their nontopographic conclusion more cleanly and so favours their idea more than Option 2, which reports only minimal differences, weak borders, and moderate similarity. Option 1 therefore better supports the authors' claim.

The authors' idea is that the 3D structural architecture of the human hand area is nontopographic, supporting flexibility of finger organization. Option 1 reports minimal structural differences, weakly delineated borders, and moderate similarity between fingers, which are more compatible with nontopography than Option 2's absence of differences, absence of borders, and high similarity. Option 2's wording is more absolute, which makes it a stronger confirmation of nontopography, so Option 2 favours the authors' idea more. Option 1 is therefore less favoured.

The authors' hypothesis is that upregulated CRHR1 in PVN presympathetic neurons drives hyperactivity and elevated sympathetic outflow in SHRs. Option 1 supports this directly: CRH produces a larger excitatory response in SHRs than WKY, and CRHR blockade reduces firing, ABP and RSNA specifically in SHRs, not WKY. Option 2 reverses these comparisons (less CRH response in SHRs, blockade effective only in WKY), which undercuts the claim that CRHR1 upregulation underlies SHR hyperactivity. Both share the same colocalization and PSD-95 data, so the difference lies in the group-specific effects, which favour Option 1.

The authors' hypothesis is that upregulated CRHR1 in the PVN drives hyperactivity of presympathetic neurons and elevated sympathetic outflow in hypertension. Option 1 reports CRH having a weaker effect in SHRs than WKY rats and CRHR blockade affecting only WKY animals, which undermines a role for CRH in SHR hyperactivity. Option 2 reports a stronger CRH effect in SHRs and CRHR blockade reducing firing, ABP and RSNA specifically in SHRs, which supports the hypothesis. Option 2 therefore favours the authors' idea more.

Both abstracts report the same core claim: intra-VTA CB1R blockade decreases sign-tracking and shifts dopamine responses in the NAc. The hypothesis is that VTA CB1R signaling regulates NAc dopamine to control sign tracking. Option 1 reports the dopamine effect in the NAc shell and in female rats, with the behavioral shift described as decreased lever and increased food cup approach. Option 2 reports the effect in the NAc core and in male rats, with the behavioral shift reversed in direction of lever/food cup. The mechanistic claim of a dopamine-behavior link is equally supported in both; the discriminating details concern anatomical specificity and behavioral direction, which do not clearly favour one version over the other. Option 1 describes the behavior shift consistent with the sign-tracking interpretation (decreased lever approach, the marker of sign-tracking), so it aligns slightly more directly with the authors' idea that CB1R blockade reduces sign-tracking.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis (VTA CB1R signaling regulates NAc dopamine to control sign tracking) and the same overall framing. Option 1 reports the sign-tracking shift toward lever approach with AM251, increased NAc core dopamine during US delivery, in male rats, with a clearer dissociation between core and shell. Option 2 uses rimonabant, reports the behavioral shift in the opposite direction in wording (decreased lever, increased food cup, which is a less intuitive reading of sign-tracking), and finds the effect in NAc shell in female rats, which is a less clean match to the hypothesis of a core-linked mechanism. The inconsistency between the behavioral direction described and the sign-tracking interpretation makes Option 1's findings more coherent with the authors' stated idea.

The authors' idea is that intrinsic neural timescales increase along the auditory hierarchy and explain response latencies. Option 1 reports timescales increasing from temporal cortex to entorhinal, hippocampal and amygdala regions, with timescales tracking onset and peak latencies. This matches the hypothesis of a hierarchy of increasing timescales linked to sensory processing latency, so it better supports the authors' idea. Option 2 reports the opposite direction and links only onset and offset latencies, weakening the claimed relationship.

The authors' hypothesis is that intrinsic neural timescales at rest hierarchically shape auditory processing, specifically that timescales predict response latency. Option 1 reports timescales decreasing along the hierarchy and decreasing with onset and offset latencies, a coherent link consistent with faster intrinsic dynamics supporting faster responses. Option 2 reports timescales increasing along the hierarchy and with onset and peak latencies, which runs against the framing that timescales facilitate processing at multiple stages, and it also reports a different latency measure. Option 1 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

The two abstracts differ in two findings: Option 1 reports other synaptic proteins unchanged and soluble Aβ42 increased, while Option 2 reports other synaptic proteins increased and soluble Aβ40 increased. The authors' hypothesis is that Shank3 deficiency contributes to cognitive impairment in AD, which is most directly supported by a clean, specific effect: Shank3a loss alone without compensatory changes, and elevation of the more pathogenic Aβ42 species. Option 1's findings align more coherently with a deleterious Shank3 deficiency story, since unchanged compensation means the deficit is not masked and Aβ42 is the more toxic peptide. Option 2's increases in other synaptic proteins would suggest compensation that weakens the narrative, though the net effect on the hypothesis is modest.

Both abstracts share the same core hypothesis and behavioral findings. The differences: Option 1 reports other synaptic proteins (PSD-95, drebrin, homer1) increased in Shank3-deficient animals, which is a compensatory finding that is less directly supportive of a clean Shank3-deficiency story; Option 2 reports them unchanged, which better isolates Shank3 loss as the driver. Option 1 reports increased soluble Aβ40, whereas Option 2 reports increased soluble Aβ42, the more pathogenic species most closely tied to AD, which more strongly supports the authors' idea that Shank3 deficiency worsens AD neuropathology. Thus Option 2's findings favour the authors' hypothesis more.

The authors' idea is that visible dying-neuron counts are a poor, confounded measure of neuronal death because the queue is sensitive to phagocytosis rate and membrane permeability. Option 1 shows that altering phagocytosis and permeability dramatically changes dying-neuron counts and that phagocytosis is overwhelmed, directly supporting this queue-artifact argument. Option 2 shows phagocytosis is sustained and manipulating it does not change counts, which undercuts the idea that the queue is sensitive to clearance rate. Option 1's findings therefore favour the authors' hypothesis more strongly.

The authors' idea is that the visible dying-neuron count is a poor, confounded measure of neuronal death because it depends equally on phagocytosis rate and membrane permeability. Option 1 supports this directly: phagocytosis capacity is sustained and altering phagocytosis or stain permeability does not change the count of dying neurons, showing the measure is decoupled from death itself. Option 2 instead shows the count changing dramatically with phagocytosis and permeability, which would be consistent with the count being sensitive to clearance, but it also reports that phagocytosis is overwhelmed, which is less aligned with a clean demonstration of confounding. Option 1 therefore better matches the authors' argument that the queue measure is misleading, though the authors' framing of sensitivity to both factors is satisfied by either version to some degree.

The two abstracts differ only in which electrode (anodal vs cathodal) strongly activates pyramidal and basket cells and which electrode Martinotti cells prefer. The authors' idea is that asymmetric activation of interneurons produces a unidirectional traveling wave. Neither version is clearly better supported by its findings; both describe the same mechanism with polarity swapped, so the support for the hypothesis is equivalent.

The two abstracts differ only in which electrode polarity (cathodal vs. anodal) preferentially activates pyramidal/basket cells and Martinotti cells. Both versions report the same qualitative outcome: a unidirectional traveling wave propagating away from the array via asymmetric interneuron activation. The authors' hypothesis (asymmetric stimulation induces directional traveling waves via interneuron asymmetry) is supported equally well in either version, so neither findings set favours the idea more than the other.

The authors' idea is that two residues form a proton-sensitive site and that PAC knockout mice resist chloral hydrate effects. Option 1 says the residues 'cooperatively' form the site, supported by double-mutant cycle analysis, which is the classic evidence for interacting residues and strengthens a cooperative-site model. It also reports KO mice resist sedation, which supports the drug-target claim. Option 2 says the residues act 'independently' and that KO mice 'respond to' chloral hydrate, undermining the drug-target claim. Option 1's findings better favour the authors' idea.

The authors' idea is a proton-sensitive site formed by two residues. Option 1 reports that the two residues 'independently' form the site, which is a weaker, less specific claim; Option 2 reports they 'cooperatively' form it, which better supports a single coherent pocket that the double-mutant cycle analysis is designed to test. Option 2 also reports that PAC KO mice 'resist' chloral hydrate sedation, which is a clearer, more consistent in vivo support for the drug-target hypothesis than Option 1's 'respond to' wording. Overall Option 2's findings favour the authors' idea more.

The two abstracts differ only in the locomotor and psychostimulant findings: Option 1 reports hyperactivity and increased sensitivity to psychostimulants, while Option 2 reports hypoactivity and decreased sensitivity. The authors' idea is that CUL3 deficiency disrupts DA neuron function and produces DA-relevant psychiatric-like behaviors, consistent with the enhanced DA signaling and elevated VTA excitability both versions share. Option 1's hyperactivity and heightened psychostimulant sensitivity align more directly with enhanced DA signaling and with the dopamine-hyperfunction model of schizophrenia and ASD that the authors invoke, so it supports their idea more coherently.

The authors' idea is that CUL3 deficiency enhances dopamine signaling and DA neuron excitability, producing psychiatric-relevant behaviors. Both versions share the DA signaling enhancement, elevated VTA excitability, haloperidol attenuation, and chemogenetic rescue. The difference is behavioral: Option 1 reports hypoactivity and decreased psychostimulant sensitivity, while Option 2 reports hyperactivity and increased psychostimulant sensitivity. Hyperactivity and heightened psychostimulant response are the phenotypes expected from elevated dopamine signaling, so Option 2's findings fit the authors' hypothesis better and would please them more.

The two abstracts differ only in anatomical locations: Option 1 places ownership in posterior parietal and agency in superior temporal cortex, while Option 2 places ownership in posterior temporal and agency in superior parietal cortex. The authors' hypothesis is that ownership and agency have distinct but overlapping neural bases, with a dorsal premotor overlap, and both versions preserve that same core claim. Neither version's findings clearly support the authors' idea more than the other, since the distinction and overlap claims are identical; the regional swaps do not change the strength of the conclusion.

The two abstracts are identical except that Option 1 reports ownership linked to posterior temporal regions and agency to superior parietal cortex, while Option 2 reports ownership linked to posterior parietal regions and agency to superior temporal cortex. The authors' idea is that ownership and agency are dissociable, with distinct neural bases and partial overlap in dorsal premotor cortex. Option 1's anatomical assignments (ownership to temporal, agency to parietal) match the common dorsal-stream/ventral-stream framing where agency relates to parietal sensorimotor integration and ownership to temporal-parietal body representation, giving a cleaner dissociation. Option 2 assigns both ownership and agency partly to parietal/temporal regions in an overlapping fashion, which weakens the claimed distinctness. Thus Option 1's findings modestly better support the authors' dissociation claim.

The two abstracts differ only in which frequency band is assigned to which brain regions: Option 1 links α to left temporal regions and β to frontal/parietal/motor regions, while Option 2 reverses this. The authors' idea is that α and β oscillations generalize from perceptual to higher-level linguistic processing, with α associated with inhibition of task-irrelevant networks and β with reactivation of content representations. Neither version's regional mapping is clearly more consistent with that framing, since both describe the same dynamics generalizing to language. Because the findings favour the authors' idea roughly equally in either version, the answer is near the midpoint.

The two abstracts are identical except for the region-frequency mapping. Option 1 assigns left temporal language regions to β and frontal/parietal/motor regions to α; Option 2 reverses this. The authors' idea is that α and β oscillations generalize to higher-level language processing, with α linked to inhibition of task-irrelevant networks and β to reactivation of content representations. Neither version clearly fits this framework better: both report dependency effects in language regions in both bands and both state the same generalization claim. The choice of which band maps to which region does not obviously strengthen or weaken the inhibition/reactivation account, so the findings are roughly equally favourable to the authors' idea.

The two abstracts differ only in which early sensory region shows the partisanship-dependent effects: Option 1 reports synchronization in primary visual and auditory cortices and sensorimotor involvement, while Option 2 reports synchronization in primary motor and somatosensory cortices and visual cortex involvement. The authors' idea is that political polarization reflects fundamental early neural mechanisms; both versions equally support this claim, with no clear difference in strength of evidence, so neither clearly favours the authors' idea more.

Both abstracts share the same design, sample, and conclusions; they differ only in which early regions show partisanship-dependent synchronization and involvement. Option 1 reports motor and somatosensory synchronization and visual cortex involvement, while Option 2 reports visual and auditory synchronization and sensorimotor involvement. The authors' idea is that political polarization reflects fundamental early sensory-level neural mechanisms; neither version clearly supports this more strongly, as both describe early sensory differences equally. Option 1's more specific visual-cortex claim could be read as a slightly more direct sensory-processing account, but this is marginal, so the answer is near neutral.

The authors' idea is that motion-selective associative areas mature on a differential trajectory relative to other occipital regions, with MT+ and V6 being the key motion areas. Option 1 reports MT+ and PIVC showing similar responses at 5 and 8 weeks, with V6 reduced, while Option 2 reports V6 and PIVC similar and MT+ reduced. Since MT+ is the canonical motion area and the authors' framing emphasizes motion-area maturation, Option 1's finding of mature MT+ responses at 5 weeks supports their idea of early motion-area development more strongly. Option 2's reduced MT+ response would weaken that claim. The two abstracts are otherwise identical, so this single difference determines the comparison.

The two abstracts differ only in which area (V6 or MT+) shows reduced BOLD response at 5 weeks. The authors' idea is a differential developmental trajectory of motion areas versus other occipital regions, which holds in both versions. Neither version clearly favours the authors' framing more; the swap of V6 and MT+ does not strengthen or weaken the central claim, so the answer is neutral.

The two abstracts differ only in one swap: Option 1 says AC neurons show heterogeneous AM rate tuning but stereotyped temporal dynamics, while Option 2 says the reverse. The authors' stated idea is that the diversity across neurons' AM responses contributes to the population representation of envelopes, and their conclusions rest on a population code with a stereotyped encoding bias (phase accumulation at AM onsets and over-representation of edges) that aids decoding. Option 1's findings, with stereotyped temporal dynamics underlying the shared edge-biased population code and heterogeneous rate tuning supporting diversity, align more directly with the authors' emphasis on diversity and the population read-out. This favours Option 1 moderately.

The two abstracts differ only in one swap: Option 1 says AC neurons show stereotyped rate tuning but heterogeneous temporal dynamics, while Option 2 says heterogeneous rate tuning but stereotyped temporal dynamics. The authors' stated idea is that the apparent diversity across neurons' AM responses contributes to the population representation of envelopes. That diversity is framed as the key finding, so the version where diversity lies in temporal dynamics (Option 1) better matches the claim that heterogeneous responses carry envelope information, since the phase accumulation and edge over-representation findings rest on temporal response differences. Option 2 shifts diversity to rate tuning, which weakens the emphasis on temporal diversity. Thus Option 1 favours the authors' idea somewhat more.

The two abstracts differ only in which theta band is described as the common, domain-general correlate. Option 1 reports slow theta (2.5-5 Hz) as shared across what, where, and when, with fast theta specific to spatial and temporal distance, which fits the authors' idea of a common conceptual mapping mechanism operating alongside domain-specific processes. Option 2 reports fast theta as the common marker and slow theta as domain-specific, which is a less natural fit for the authors' framing. Neither version is clearly stronger on every point, but Option 1's assignment supports the authors' hypothesis of shared slow-theta mapping more directly.

The two abstracts differ only in which theta band is labeled as domain-general (common across what, where, when) versus domain-specific. Option 1 assigns the common cross-domain correlate to fast theta (5-8.5 Hz) and spatial/temporal specificity to slow theta, while Option 2 reverses this. The authors' idea is that both domain-general and domain-specific processes co-occur; neither version clearly supports this better, as the structure and claims are otherwise identical. Neither option is more favorable to the authors' hypothesis, so the probability is near even.

The two abstracts differ only in which response attention enhances: Option 1 says attention enhanced the event-related response to the transient auditory deviants, while Option 2 says it enhanced the event-related response to the visual stimulus. The study's stated aim is to show dissociable bottom-up (coherence) and top-down (attention) signatures in audiovisual object formation, with coherence affecting auditory envelope responses and attention affecting a separate event-related response. Option 1 keeps the dissociation within the auditory modality, consistent with the framing of auditory selective attention and envelope tracking. Option 2 attributes attention's effect to the visual stimulus, which the task rendered task-irrelevant, making the dissociation story less coherent. Option 1 therefore more clearly supports the authors' idea.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis: that bottom-up AV coherence and top-down attention have dissociable neural signatures. The only difference is the response that attention enhances: Option 1 reports the event-related response evoked by the visual stimulus, while Option 2 reports the response evoked by the transient auditory deviants. Option 1's finding supports dissociation only partially, since the visual response is a neutral signal relative to the auditory coherence result. Option 2's finding, that attention enhances responses to the very deviants participants were detecting while coherence does not, more cleanly matches the claimed bottom-up/top-down dissociation and is the more task-relevant measure. Hence Option 2 favours the authors' idea somewhat more.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis: that numerosity maps are involved in symbolic number processing. The only difference is the hemisphere where numerosity-tuned populations are shown to respond to symbolic numbers: Option 1 reports the left hemisphere, Option 2 the right. Neither version is clearly stronger for the authors' idea on its face, since the core claim and sample are identical. The authors' support is equivalent across both, so the likelihood is near even.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis: that numerosity maps are involved in symbolic number processing. The only difference is the hemisphere where numerosity-tuned populations are reported to be tuned to symbolic numbers (right in Option 1, left in Option 2). Option 1 reports this in the right hemisphere, which matches the phrasing of the NTO-map finding and the claimed link, so it slightly better supports the authors' idea, though the difference is small.

The two abstracts differ only in the direction of the MD activation group difference and the hemisphere emphasized for the performance relationship. Option 1 reports lower MD activation in children and right-hemisphere effects; Option 2 reports higher MD activation in children and left-hemisphere effects. The authors' hypothesis is that MD regions are selective to cognitive demand, distinct from language cortex, and sensitive to ability even in children. Both versions support this equally on the core claims (distinctness from language, performance relationship holding across age). The directional difference in activation does not clearly favour the authors' idea either way, so neither version clearly better supports the hypothesis.

The authors' idea is that the MD network is selective to cognitive demand, distinct from language cortex, and sensitive to ability even in children. Option 1 reports MD activation higher in children than adults and a left-hemisphere ability relationship; Option 2 reports lower child activation and a right-hemisphere relationship. Neither version's core claims (bilateral MD activation, distinctness from language, ability-related increases) differ in a way that clearly favours one, though the directional child-vs-adult difference is a side detail. Option 1's finding of higher child activation fits a developmental-compensation narrative sometimes used to argue early emergence, while the hemispheric detail is incidental. Overall the difference is marginal, leaning slightly toward Option 1.

The authors' idea is that serial-dependence biases arise at sensory processing and can be overridden postperceptually. Option 1 reports neural repulsion during encoding with behavioral attraction, consistent with a sensory-level repulsive bias that is overridden later to produce attraction. Option 2 reports neural attraction with behavioral repulsion, which is the mirror image and does not show the intended dissociation in the same direction. Option 1's pattern more cleanly supports the authors' stated framework, so it favours the authors' idea more.

The authors hypothesize that serial biases arise at the level of sensory processing and can be overridden postperceptually. Option 1 reports neural attractive biases during encoding and behavioral repulsive biases, consistent with attractive sensory biases being overridden later. Option 2 reports neural repulsive biases during encoding and behavioral attractive biases, which would be consistent with the same story but with the directions swapped. Neither option is clearly stronger for the authors' idea, since both show a dissociation between sensory-level and behavioral biases, so the support is essentially equivalent.

The authors' idea is that post-choice HPC activity conveys retrospective signals to PFC, which supports rule formation and faster learning. Option 1 reports PFC tracking current goal better than start location, CA1-predicted PFC changes correlating with faster learning, and PFC start-arm modulation correlating with slower learning, all consistent with that account. Option 2 reverses the learning-rate correlations and the PFC tracking comparison, undercutting the proposed HPC-to-PFC signalling role. Option 1 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

The authors' idea is that post-choice HPC activity conveys retrospective signals to the PFC that build rules, with PFC modulation supporting learning. Option 1 reports that CA1 post-choice activity predicting PFC change correlates with slower learning, and PFC start-arm modulation of CA1 correlates with faster learning, and that PFC tracks past start location worse than current goal. Option 2 reports that CA1-to-PFC prediction correlates with faster learning and PFC start-arm modulation with slower learning, with PFC tracking current goal better. Option 2's findings align more closely with a framework where HPC retrospective signals drive rule formation and faster learning, and where PFC tracks goals, so Option 2 better supports the authors' idea.

Both abstracts test the same hypothesis, a medial-to-lateral gradient in which lateral hemispheres support higher-level social inference and medial/vermal sectors support basic emotion perception. Option 1's findings match that hypothesis: medial TMS impairs basic emotion recognition and lateral TMS affects the social-context task, supporting the gradient as predicted. Option 2 reverses the pattern, showing a lateral-to-medial gradient that contradicts the authors' stated framework, so it supports the idea less. Option 1 clearly favours the authors' idea.

The authors hypothesized a medial-to-lateral gradient, with lateral (phylogenetically newer) hemispheres supporting higher-level social inference and medial/vermal sectors supporting basic perceptual emotion processing. Option 2 reports exactly this pattern: medial TMS impairs basic emotion recognition and lateral TMS affects contextual, mentalizing-type recognition, with the summary explicitly claiming a medial-to-lateral gradient. Option 1 reports the reverse (lateral for basic, medial for higher inference) and concludes a lateral-to-medial gradient, contradicting the hypothesis. So Option 2's findings favour the authors' idea more.

The two abstracts are identical except for the final sentence. Option 1 reports that the best results came from the combined AAV-NG2Ab+AAV-NT3 treatment, which supports the authors' hypothesis that neutralizing NG2 inhibition is optimal and that combining it with a neurotrophin adds benefit. Option 2 reports the best results came from AAV-NG2Ab alone, which still supports neutralizing NG2 but does not show the added benefit of combination therapy. Option 1 therefore makes the authors' idea look somewhat better supported.

The authors hypothesized that neutralizing NG2's inhibitory function with anti-NG2 antibody (AAV-NG2Ab) is the optimal treatment. Option 1 reports the best results for AAV-NG2Ab alone, which directly supports the idea that antibody neutralization alone is the optimal strategy. Option 2 reports the best results for the combination with NT-3, which would suggest NT-3 co-delivery adds benefit and weakens the claim that neutralization alone is optimal. Both versions show significant improvements over control, but Option 1 aligns more closely with the authors' stated hypothesis.

The authors propose that meningeal P2X7 and Pannexin 1 signaling mediates CSD-evoked mechanical sensitization of meningeal afferents. Option 1 reports that blocking P2X7/Pannexin 1 suppresses this sensitization and that P2X7 signaling does not affect CSD susceptibility, which directly supports a specific, pronociceptive role for the pathway without confounding effects on cortical excitability. Option 2 reports that blockade enhances sensitization (opposite to the proposed pronociceptive role) and that P2X7 signaling increases CSD susceptibility, which contradicts the hypothesis. Option 1 therefore makes the authors' idea look better supported.

The authors propose that meningeal P2X7 and Pannexin 1 signaling mediates CSD-evoked mechanical sensitization of meningeal afferents. Option 1 reports that P2X7/Pannexin 1 blockade enhances sensitization, which contradicts the proposed pronociceptive role, and reports that P2X7 signaling increases CSD susceptibility, which is an additional finding. Option 2 reports that blockade suppresses sensitization, consistent with the hypothesis that P2X7/Pannexin 1 signaling drives mechanical sensitization, and reports no effect on CSD susceptibility. Option 2's findings therefore favour the authors' idea more clearly.

The authors' idea is that semantic information alters early and late visual and semantic processing, with effects appearing immediately. Option 1 reports larger N170, reduced N400, decreased alpha/beta power, and increased P1 for semantically informed objects. Option 2 reports the opposite direction for each component. Neither version is inherently more supportive of a general claim that semantic information changes perception, since both describe effects at all stages; the study's main claim is equally supported by either direction. The question asks which findings favour the idea more, and the directional differences are arbitrary with respect to the stated hypothesis, so the answer is near neutral.

Both abstracts describe the same study and the same proposed idea: that semantic information alters visual perception across processing stages. The authors' idea is that semantic information changes perception, which is supported by any reliable differences between informed and uninformed conditions regardless of direction. Option 1 reports effects in the directions framed as consistent with prior work (reduced P1 and N170, increased N400), while Option 2 reports the opposite signs. Neither version is clearly more supportive of the hypothesis in a way that would differ by direction alone, so the findings are roughly equally favourable, with a slight edge to Option 1 only because its pattern is described as the expected direction from previous work.

The authors' idea is that SSA mediates deviance-driven distraction affecting perception. Option 1 reports faster reactions with worse target detection, which is a clear distraction effect consistent with the hypothesis that deviants capture attention and impair detection. Option 2 reports slower reactions with improved detection, which is not a distraction effect in the expected direction and weakens the proposed mechanism. Option 1 also localises the correlation to deeper layers, which is less informative than shallow but both are layer-specific. Overall Option 1 better supports the authors' idea.

The two abstracts differ in the direction of the behavioral effect (Option 1: slower reaction times but improved target detection; Option 2: faster reaction times but worsened detection) and in the cortical layers where deviant-triggered distraction correlates with neural responses (Option 1: shallower layers; Option 2: deeper layers). The authors' idea is that SSA shapes perception in a layer-specific way; Option 1 reports a benefit to detection and a shallow-layer link, which more directly supports a perceptual role for SSA in the sense of enhanced signal salience, whereas Option 2 reports a detriment. Option 1 therefore better supports the authors' framing of SSA as a mechanism of exogenous attentional capture that tunes perception.

The authors' framing emphasizes PL as an integral contributor that biases and integrates decision signals; both versions share this framing. Option 1 reports prechoice suppression reducing bias toward preferred options and inhibition during reward receipt reducing risky choice, which fits a view of PL signals as reinforcing rewarded risky choices and driving relative value comparison. Option 2 reports the opposite directions for these effects (increased bias, increased risky choice). The authors' multifaceted account of PL contributions is more naturally supported by Option 1's pattern of disruption effects, which matches the proposed reinforcing and comparator roles, though neither version is clearly stronger on every point.

Both abstracts report the same design and mostly the same narrative. The key difference is the direction of effects. Option 1 reports that prechoice PL suppression increased bias toward preferred options and that inhibition during reward receipt increased risky choice when risky was more profitable. Option 2 reports the opposite directions for these effects. The authors' idea is that PL signals act as a relative value comparator and reinforce rewarded risky choices, which is a claim that PL signals drive choice in a particular direction. Both versions are internally coherent with that framing, so neither clearly favours the authors' idea more than the other in terms of their stated hypothesis; the findings are simply mirrored. Judging from the framing that PL signals augment incentive and reinforce rewarded risky choices, Option 2's reported reduction in risky choice upon inhibition fits less naturally with a reinforcing role, while Option 1's increase in risky choice under inhibition during rewards is somewhat less consistent with the 'reinforce' claim as well, so the balance is near even.

The two versions differ only in whether the context-modulated place memory patches lie anterior or posterior to the scene perception areas. The authors' framework (Steel, Baldassano, Epstein, Robertson) builds on prior work showing place memory areas sit immediately anterior to scene perception areas, with perception posterior and memory anterior as an organizing principle. Anterior findings replicate and extend that idea; posterior findings would contradict it. So Option 1 favours the authors' hypothesis.

The authors (Steel, Robertson and colleagues) have a known hypothesis that place memory areas lie immediately anterior to scene perception areas, interleaved with them as a systematic organization, and they identify these as the convergence zone. Option 2 reports anterior patches, matching this prior framework. Option 1 reports posterior patches, which contradicts the established anterior place-memory area finding and would be an unexpected result for their idea. Option 2 therefore better supports the authors' hypothesis.

The authors hypothesized that the CeA-PBN pathway, known to regulate pain, also controls itch. Both versions support pathway involvement, but Option 1 shows a coherent inhibitory effect: stimulation reduces scratching, suppresses PBN Fos, and raises pain thresholds (analgesia), consistent with the prior pain-regulation finding and an amygdala-mediated antipruritic/analgesic role. Option 2 gives the opposite direction (pro-itch, hyperalgesia) and has an internally inconsistent Fos result (decreased Fos after chloroquine yet enhanced with stimulation). Option 1 fits the prior literature and the hypothesis better.

The authors hypothesize that the Pdyn+ CeA-PBN pathway, previously implicated in pain regulation, also controls itch. Both versions support regulation of itch, so both confirm the hypothesis. Option 2 is more internally coherent: stimulation inhibits scratching, chloroquine increases PBN Fos, stimulation suppresses it, and thresholds rise (analgesia). That parallels the known analgesic CeA-PBN role and a coherent inhibitory story. Option 1 has stimulation increasing itch and lowering thresholds (hyperalgesia), which conflicts with the prior pain-regulation finding and contains an odd Fos pattern. Option 2 fits the 'same pathway' idea slightly better.

The framing stresses 'cellular heterogeneity' as the obscuring gap, and the authors seem to want to show endothelial diversity and AD-specific changes. Option 1 reports regional heterogeneity, distinct responses to amyloid pathology, and upregulated protein folding genes, supporting an active endothelial role in AD. Option 2 reports homogeneity and similar responses, which undercuts the premise of heterogeneity and the novelty of the dataset.

The authors framed the study around limited understanding of endothelial 'cellular heterogeneity' in aged and AD brain, and they built a large multi-region dataset to resolve it. Finding regional heterogeneity, region-specific signatures, and distinct responses to amyloid pathology (Option 2) would validate that premise and make the dataset seem more valuable. Option 1's homogeneity is a null-ish result, though it is framed as a 'previously unrecognized' finding. Option 2 likely pleases the authors more, though both are publishable.

The authors frame their work as supporting computational models that ascribe a fundamental role to hippocampal theta in memory, and as evaluating the Herweg et al. masking hypothesis. Option 1 shows narrowband theta increasing during successful encoding and before recall, with broadband decreases masking it, matching both the models and the masking idea. Option 2 reports theta decreases, which contradicts the rodent-model-based expectation, making the 'in line with computational models' claim incoherent.

The authors test Herweg et al.'s hypotheses that broadband decreases mask narrowband theta increases, and frame their result as 'in line with computational models' ascribing a fundamental role to theta. Option 2 shows narrowband theta increasing during encoding and retrieval, consistent with rodent models and Herweg's masking idea. Option 1 shows theta decreases, which contradicts the hypotheses yet is still framed as supportive, which is awkward. Option 2 fits the narrative far better.

The authors want to show motion cues robustly drive category responses, even in ventral regions traditionally tied to form. Option 1 says ventral/posterior regions favor static while dorsal/anterior favor dynamic, matching the classic ventral-form versus dorsal-motion framework, but still shows robust ventral motion decoding. Option 2 reverses this: ventral/posterior regions show higher accuracy for motion-defined stimuli, which more strongly supports the surprising claim that motion drives ventral category responses. Option 2 also has an odd 'dynamic luminance cues' wording, but findings-wise it favors the authors' idea more.

The authors want to show motion cues elicit robust category responses, even in ventral regions traditionally tied to form processing. Option 1 reports higher motion-defined (dynamic) decoding in posterior occipitotemporal and ventral regions, directly supporting that claim and the surprising ventral involvement. Option 2 has dynamic advantage only in anterior and dorsal regions, which fits the conventional dorsal/motion view and is less striking. Option 1 favours the authors' idea more.

The authors' central idea is that PrL activity underlies distress tolerance and links to drug-seeking. Both versions support this equally, differing only in which sex shows the effects. Neither sex-specific outcome clearly favors the hypothesis more. Human literature on DT and drug-seeking has no strong sex-specific prior that would make one outcome better supported. A slight lean might exist for females, given the prevalence of female-focused DT work, but this is weak.

The authors' core idea is that PrL activity underlies distress tolerance and links to drug-seeking. Both versions support this equally; they differ only in whether the effect appears in females or males. No hypothesis in the abstract specifies a sex. Human DT literature shows low DT linked to drug use in both sexes, and female-specific findings fit the prevailing narrative of heightened female vulnerability to cocaine seeking and relapse in rodents, so Option 1 is slightly more consistent with prior expectations. Neither clearly favors the idea more.

The authors' idea is that the stochastic framework with mean/covariance decomposition is useful. Both versions show dissociation. Option 1 (visual areas control means, PCC controls covariances) is more plausible: visual areas show strong task-evoked activation changes (means), while PCC, a default-mode hub, is tied to connectivity/covariance changes. This fits prior knowledge, making the framework's results look more credible.

The two versions differ only in swapping which regions control means versus covariances. Option 1 (lower visual areas control covariances, PCC controls means) is more consistent with prior knowledge: the PCC is a high-activation default-mode hub whose task-related mean deactivation is well known, while visual areas show task-driven variance/connectivity changes. This makes Option 1 look more sensible and better validate the framework, though the preference is modest.

The authors' core idea is that age-related fluid intelligence decline is mediated by frontoparietal responsiveness to novel problem-solving, building on the premise that fluid intelligence depends on activation of this network. Option 1 shows mediation tied to voxels most activated by demand, which fits this activation-based framing. Option 2 ties mediation to suppressed (deactivated) voxels, which sits awkwardly with the activation-centered hypothesis. The physical-activity moderation differences (variety vs frequency) are roughly neutral. Option 1 therefore supports the authors' idea better.

The authors' hypothesis is that age-related declines in fluid intelligence are mediated by frontoparietal activation during problem-solving, which the framing in both versions emphasizes as activation of the frontoparietal network. Option 2 localizes mediation to voxels most activated by demand, which fits the stated hypothesis directly. Option 1 finds mediation only in voxels most suppressed by demand (deactivation), a less expected result that sits less comfortably with the 'activation' framing. The moderation findings (frequency vs variety) are exploratory and roughly neutral. Option 2 modestly favors the authors' idea more.

Both versions fit a mutual-inhibition story, so neither is clearly better supported. Option 1 has danger shifting consolidation to the BLA, which fits the established view that fear and danger engage the amygdala. Option 2 has danger shifting it to the PRh, which is a more surprising pattern. Option 1 is also more consistent with the prior literature on PRh in neutral recognition memory and BLA in emotional memory. The authors likely favor the more coherent narrative of Option 1, but only slightly.

The two options swap the roles of PRh and BLA. Option 1 has danger shifting consolidation from BLA to PRh, with early pairings encoded in PRh and later ones in BLA. This fits the discussion of mutually inhibitory PRh-BLA interactions and PRh's role in recognition memory: danger suppresses later BLA-dependent traces and preserves the PRh-dependent early trace, an account the authors' framing suggests. Option 2 reverses the direction, which seems less consistent with PRh's known role in novelty/familiarity of early exposures and with the stated link to recognition memory. Option 1 appears more likely the authors' idea.

Option 1 is internally coherent and matches known developmental biology: frontal connections mature later, a posterior-to-anterior gradient, and faster lateral thalamic growth consistent with a lateral-to-medial pattern. Option 2 is internally inconsistent: frontal connections develop earlier yet a posterior-to-anterior gradient is claimed, and the lateral thalamus is described as slower while partitions develop lateral-to-medial. Option 1's findings fit the authors' framework far better.

The authors' idea is a descriptive developmental pattern, so support depends on internal coherence. Option 2 is coherent: faster lateral development matches the lateral-to-medial partition maturation, and later frontal connectivity matches a posterior-to-anterior gradient. Option 1 is inconsistent: it reports earlier frontal development yet claims a posterior-to-anterior gradient, and claims slower lateral development despite lateral-to-medial maturation. Option 2's findings fit together better and support the narrative more.

The authors' idea is that cortico-thalamic feedback contributes to state-dependent dLGN responses. Option 1 shows silencing feedback profoundly reduces state-dependent differences for both temporal and spatial features, directly supporting that feedback is necessary for the state effect. Option 2 reports an increase after silencing, which is inconsistent with feedback producing the state dependence, and includes muddled details (auditory stimulus, late stage, temporal not spatial). Option 1 clearly supports the hypothesis better.

The authors' hypothesis is that cortico-thalamic feedback contributes to state-dependent dLGN responses. Option 2 shows that silencing feedback reduces state-dependent differences, meaning feedback is needed for them, and the effect holds for both temporal and spatial features. Option 1 shows silencing increases the differences, which implies feedback suppresses or opposes state effects, and its text is internally odd (auditory stimulus, 'late stage'). Option 2 more cleanly supports the idea that feedback underlies state-dependent responses.

The authors cite prior work (Kremkow 2014; Rahimi-Nasrabadi 2021) showing ON cortical pathways have higher contrast sensitivity, and animal models linking ON pathway deficits to low-contrast vision loss. Option 1 (OFF dominance at high contrast, ON at low contrast) matches this literature and their framing. Option 2 reverses the pattern and would contradict the cited prior evidence, making the interpretation internally inconsistent. Option 1 better supports the authors' idea.

The authors' framework, citing Kremkow 2014 and Rahimi-Nasrabadi 2021, holds that ON cortical pathways have lower contrast sensitivity and OFF pathways dominate at low contrast. Option 1 matches this: OFF dominance at low contrast shifting to ON at high contrast, with predicted low-contrast loss from OFF deficits. Option 2 reverses the pattern and states ON pathways have higher contrast sensitivity, contradicting the cited literature and the OFF-deficit animal model. Option 1 better supports their idea.

The two versions differ only in the topography of the coherence effects. Option 1 pairs the 4-5 Hz saccade rhythm with whole-head theta and the 1 Hz fixation rhythm with occipital delta. Option 2 reverses this. Both support the authors' claim of rhythmic eye movements coupled to oscillations. Occipital delta in Option 1 fits visual-cortex involvement and the link to sentence-level chunking via sentence-ending phase-locking. A brain-wide theta effect for word-locked saccades also fits an endogenous, language-driven rhythm. Occipital theta for saccades (Option 2) is plausible too, so the difference is small, but Option 1 seems slightly more natural.

The authors argue that linguistic processing imposes endogenous rhythms. The delta-band ~1 Hz effect is tied to sentence endings and multi-word chunking, a higher-level linguistic process. A whole-head delta topography (Option 1) fits a distributed, language-related, endogenous mechanism better than an occipital one, which would look visual or sensorimotor. Conversely, theta saccade coherence being occipital (Option 1) fits a visual/oculomotor sampling account, which is plausible for word-locked saccades. Option 1 therefore maps the linguistic effect to a more fitting, widespread topography, modestly favoring the authors' idea.

The abstract states only the aim of testing whether reactivation facilitates abstraction, with no stated preference for REM or SWS. Both versions show a cue effect in one stage and neural discrimination in that stage. REM is the more novel, less-expected finding and arguably fits 'sleep facilitates abstraction' theories linking REM to creativity and integration, whereas SWS is the standard TMR stage. This slightly favors Option 1, but the difference is small.

The authors' core idea is that targeted memory reactivation can facilitate abstraction. Both versions support this, differing only in which sleep stage works. SWS is the dominant, better-established stage for memory reactivation, so the SWS finding fits prior theory and mechanistic expectations. A REM-specific result would be more surprising and less aligned with the standard framework, though still novel. Option 1 is slightly more consistent with the likely hypothesis and more convincing.

The authors invoke actor-critic models as support for their dissociation. In standard actor-critic mappings, ventral striatum/VTA is the critic (value) and dorsal striatum/SNc is the actor (action policy). Option 1 assigns VTA to motivational value (critic) and SNc to action-specific learning (actor), matching this canonical mapping and prior literature. Option 2 reverses it, which would conflict with the framework and be less satisfying.

The two versions swap the roles of VTA and SNc. Authors typically want results consistent with an established framework. The classic actor-critic mapping (O'Doherty, Takahashi) assigns the ventral striatum/VTA to the critic and the dorsal striatum/SNc to the actor. Option 2 matches this canonical mapping, with VTA as critic (motivational value) and SNc as actor (action-specific learning). Option 1 reverses it, which would be a surprising departure. The actor-critic analogy therefore fits more naturally with Option 2's findings.

The authors' idea is that pupil diameter tracks arousal-dependent neural and vascular dynamics. Option 1 matches known physiology: pupil dilation reflects higher arousal, blood volume decreases with arousal, and NREM brings vasodilation and constriction, so negative correlations at rest/NREM and positive ones when alert or in REM fit established findings. Blinking linked to arousal increases and blood volume drops during sleep is also coherent. Option 2 reverses these signs into odd, contradictory patterns (blinking decreases arousal). Option 1 supports the framework better.

The authors' core idea is that pupil diameter tracks arousal-dependent neural and vascular dynamics. Option 1 reports the physiologically expected pattern: sleep brings increased blood volume and a positive pupil-gamma-blood volume relation at rest/NREM, turning negative during alertness. Blinking during sleep brings arousal decreases and blood volume increases, consistent with the intro's sleep-related blood flow increases. Option 2 reverses signs, producing an odd pattern (blinks increasing arousal while decreasing blood volume in sleep) that conflicts with the framing. Option 1 fits better.

The abstract frames apical tonotopy as incomplete knowledge and a gap to fill. The authors' idea is not clearly stated, but the framing (assumed tonotopy, known gaps) suggests a novel finding is more appealing. Option 1 says apical responses differ across locations consistent with basal patterns, supporting the standard tonotopy view. Option 2 uses a convoluted double negative that effectively says responses show no inconsistent pattern, which is ambiguous and weaker. Option 1 is a cleaner, more affirmative confirmation of tonotopy.

The authors framed the study around filling a gap in apical tonotopy knowledge. Option 2 reports apical responses varying in a pattern consistent with base findings, which confirms the standard tonotopy framework and gives a clean, supportive result. Option 1 uses a confusing double negative that amounts to roughly the same finding (no non-conforming pattern), but it reads as a null or ambiguous result. Option 2 more clearly supports the authors' implied hypothesis of consistent tonotopy.

The authors' hypothesis is that respiration entrainment of mPFC is behavioral state-dependent. Both versions show state-dependence, so both support it equally. The difference is which state shows stronger gamma entrainment and superficial recruitment. Option 2 (stress/TS strongest) might fit an emotional-regulation narrative slightly better, but Option 1 (home cage) is equally consistent with a state-dependence claim. The abstracts differ little in how well they support the core idea.

The authors' idea is that respiration dynamically entrains prefrontal activity in a behavioral state-dependent manner. Both versions show state-dependence, so both support it equally. The difference is which state shows stronger gamma entrainment (TS vs HC) and which shows superficial recruitment. Stronger entrainment during stress (TS) is a more compelling, emotionally relevant finding, and the study's framing around stress coping slightly favors it. But the core hypothesis is supported either way, so the preference is only slight.

The authors' framing is that developmental deprivation from otitis media causes lasting central auditory changes, including in the efferent pathway, and that these changes matter for hearing in noise. Option 1 shows weaker efferent inhibition and worse speech-in-noise performance in the otitis media group, consistent with deprivation-induced deficits and with the 'hallmark of impaired central auditory processing' wording. Option 2 shows stronger inhibition and better performance, which contradicts the 'impaired' framing and the deprivation-harm hypothesis.

The authors' idea is that otitis media history alters the descending efferent system and impairs central auditory processing, with poorer speech-in-noise tied to efferent changes. Option 2 is internally coherent: weaker efferent inhibition and higher SNR required (poorer performance), consistent with 'poorer speech-in-noise recognition, a hallmark of impaired central processing.' Option 1 reports lower SNR required (better performance) yet calls it 'poorer,' which is contradictory, and stronger inhibition with better performance undermines the deficit narrative. Option 2 supports their idea more.

The authors' idea is a functional parieto-frontal V6A–premotor–M1 route during reach planning. Both versions show a short-latency functional connection at 4 ms only, so support for the pathway is equal. The difference is inhibitory versus excitatory influence. Excitatory facilitation of M1 during reach planning seems more intuitive and consistent with the idea that V6A sends target information to frontal cortex, whereas inhibition is less intuitive. Yet the authors frame inhibition as a novel 'first demonstration', so they might be fine with it. Slight edge to excitatory.

The authors hypothesize a parieto-frontal pathway where V6A sends reach-planning signals to M1 via premotor cortex. Facilitation of motor-evoked potentials is the more natural, expected signature of target/reach information flowing to motor cortex, and fits the 'excitatory signals' framing and agreement with neuroimaging. Inhibition would be a less intuitive result and harder to reconcile with the proposed transmission of planning information, though it could be spun as gating. Option 1 therefore fits their idea somewhat better.
