The authors' idea is that P2X7R plays different roles in dendritic arborization under physiological versus pathologic conditions. Option 1 shows a clear dissociation: blockade/KO under physiological conditions causes branching deficits (receptor promotes outgrowth), while pathologic activation causes deficits too, consistent with schizophrenia's known dendritic deficits. Option 2 reports surpluses in both conditions, which would not support 'different roles' and conflicts with the schizophrenia model's hallmark. So Option 1 fits better.

The authors conclude P2X7R plays different roles under physiological vs pathologic conditions. Option 1 gives opposite directions: blockade increases branching physiologically (P2X7R restrains outgrowth), while pathologic activation also increases outgrowth. That is not a clean opposing pattern. Option 2 gives deficits in both: KO reduces branching physiologically (P2X7R promotes outgrowth), and pathologic activation also reduces outgrowth, again same direction. Both are internally parallel, so the 'different roles' claim is equally awkward. Schizophrenia is typically associated with reduced dendritic arborization, so Option 2's MIA-induced deficits fit the disease model better, and deficits dependent on P2X7R are more coherent with the pathology.

The two versions differ only in the specific nodes affected: ventral striatum and VTA (Option 1) versus dorsal striatum and substantia nigra (Option 2). The authors' idea concerns dopamine-renin-angiotensin interactions modulating reward and motivational salience. The ventral striatum and VTA are the canonical mesolimbic reward circuit, so effects there fit the hypothesis more directly and more neatly than dorsal striatum and substantia nigra. Option 1 therefore looks slightly better supported, though the difference is modest.

The two versions differ only in the anatomical nodes: dorsal striatum and substantia nigra (Option 1) versus ventral striatum and ventral tegmental area (Option 2). The authors' idea is that the renin-angiotensin system modulates dopaminergic midbrain-striato-frontal circuits in social reward and punishment. Ventral striatum and VTA are the classic core reward and dopamine nodes, so Option 2's findings fit the dopamine-RAS reward hypothesis a bit more neatly. SN and dorsal striatum still count as dopaminergic, so support is similar. A slight edge goes to Option 2.

Both versions support the core idea that domain organization extends to the pulvinar; they differ only in lateralization. Option 1 (left-lateralized tools, right amygdala path for animals) matches known cortical patterns: left-lateralized tool processing (left parietal/premotor/pMTG) and right-lateralized amygdala/animal-related threat processing. This congruence with cortical organization makes the claim of an overarching domain principle more coherent. Option 2's flipped lateralization is less consistent with prior literature, weakening the narrative slightly.

The authors' idea is that domain organization (animals vs tools) extends to the pulvinar and mirrors cortical organization. Both versions show distinct pulvinar patterns and connectivity links, so the core claim is equally supported. The difference is lateralization. In the cortex, tool-preferring regions (left posterior middle temporal gyrus, left parietal) are left-lateralized, so left-lateralized pulvinar tool responses (Option 2) would match cortical organization better. Amygdala-based animal threat processing is often right-biased, also favoring Option 2. This gives Option 2 a slight edge for consistency with cortical findings.

The authors' central idea is that vSUB-NAcMS is functionally distinct from vCA1 and from total vHIPP output, so subregions must be studied separately. Both versions support this equally, since each reports vSUB is distinct and vCA1 recapitulates prior vHIPP properties. The only difference is which MSN subtype shows the bias and cocaine-induced plasticity (D2R vs D1R). Neither obviously favors the thesis more; D1R bias would match canonical reward/hyperactivity notions slightly, but D2R specificity is arguably more 'novel and distinct'. Essentially a toss-up.

The authors' central idea is that vSUB-NAcMS is functionally distinct from vCA1 and from prior vHIPP findings. Both options support this equally. They differ in D1R versus D2R bias and which synapse shows cocaine plasticity. Prior vHIPP work reported D1R-biased connectivity, so Option 1's D1R bias might match earlier vHIPP results, slightly undercutting distinctness. Option 2's D2R bias and D2R-specific plasticity contrast more clearly with prior vHIPP findings, though the abstract says vCA1 recapitulated those. Difference is small; Option 2 slightly favours the distinctness claim.

The authors' idea is that the CON splits into two subnetworks mirroring the FPN, with a dmPFC link. Option 1 assigns rostral/ventral CON to future/internal control and caudal/dorsal to present/external, which matches the known FPN rostro-caudal gradient (anterior/rostral for abstract, future-oriented control). Option 2 reverses this, which would not 'mirror' the FPN's known organization and is less coherent. Option 1 also places dmPFC (a core CON node) as the mediator, which is more plausible than vmPFC, so it fits the authors' framework better.

The two versions differ only in the anatomical mapping: caudal/dorsal vs rostral/ventral for future/internal vs present/external control, and vmPFC vs dmPFC as the mediating hub. The authors' core idea (parallel CON-FPN subnetworks) is supported equally in both. Which mapping fits better depends on the 'mirroring the FPN' claim. In the FPN literature (Nee & Brown, Badre), rostral lateral PFC supports more abstract, temporally extended control, while caudal supports immediate, concrete control. A mapping where CON mirrors this would be rostral=future/internal, caudal=present/external, favoring Option 2. Option 1's mapping is opposite and less consistent with the established rostro-caudal gradient, though it could be reconciled with other findings.

The two versions differ only in the brain region: superior colliculus (Option 1) versus inferior colliculus (Option 2). The superior colliculus is the well-established prototypical orienting circuit controlling head and gaze movements, so findings there fit the authors' framing ('prototypical orienting neural circuit') and prior literature. The inferior colliculus is an auditory structure, and claiming it controls and codes the direction of orienting movements would be surprising and less consistent with the narrative. Option 1 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

The two versions differ only in the structure studied: inferior colliculus (Option 1) versus superior colliculus (Option 2). The superior colliculus is the classic orienting circuit, so confirming it as a 'prototypical orienting neural circuit' is more natural and credible. Inferior colliculus involvement in head orienting is less established, though the auditory CS makes it plausible. The authors' idea, that state-dependent orienting modulation involves a collicular circuit, fits slightly better with the superior colliculus.

The authors' idea is that rsFC changes after dynamic adaptation reflect consolidation. Option 1 reports increased cortico-cerebellar rsFC after adaptation, matching the standard expectation that learning/consolidation strengthens connectivity, and the literature on cerebellar-cortical coupling after motor learning. Option 2 reports decreases, which are less intuitive and harder to interpret as consolidation, though still reported as functionally meaningful. Option 1 fits the consolidation hypothesis more cleanly.

Both versions support the authors' idea that the cortico-cerebellar network has a functional role in consolidation, with the same behavioral associations; only the direction of rsFC change is flipped. Increases in connectivity after learning are the more conventional expectation for consolidation, so Option 2 may look slightly more intuitive. However, decreases in cortico-cerebellar rsFC are also reported in prior motor learning work, so Option 1 is equally plausible. The difference in support is minimal.

Option 1 matches the more plausible developmental narrative: children, who are still learning social understanding, rely on effortful mental-state inference via the mentalizing network, while adults use efficient, automatic body and biological motion processing. The interpretation about 'learning to better understand others' fits children. In Option 2, the same learning rationale is attached to adults, which is incoherent. Option 1's findings fit a coherent, theoretically expected story and would please the authors more.

The authors' interpretation ties to the findings: in Option 1, children rely on efficient body/biological motion processing while adults use mentalizing inference, a story consistent with the framing that adults use hidden mental state inferences 'as a potential means of learning'. The phrase 'learning to better understand' fits Option 2's narrative of children relying on mentalizing, but Option 1 matches the common developmental view that children rely on lower-level perceptual cues and mentalizing matures later. Option 1 is more plausible and likely the real result.

The authors' idea is that astrocytes in the basal forebrain contribute to sleep homeostasis, so that sleep need depends on specific neuronal-glial circuits and not merely on time awake. Option 1 shows long, continuous wakefulness without a homeostatic rebound, and rules out ligand off-target effects, which cleanly supports a dissociation between wake and sleep drive. Option 2 shows fragmented wake (little sleep loss) and attributes the effect to ligand artifacts, which undermines the interpretation. Option 1 clearly supports the authors' hypothesis better.

The authors' idea is that sleep need depends on specific neuronal-glial circuits, not wakefulness per se. Option 2 shows long continuous wakefulness with no homeostatic rebound, and rules out ligand off-target effects, so the dissociation is cleanly attributed to astrocyte circuit activation. Option 1 gives short, fragmented wake (weaker sleep loss, so no rebound is less surprising) and attributes the result to indirect ligand effects, undermining the astrocyte interpretation. Option 2 supports the hypothesis better.

The authors aim to show that MT is efficient and reconcile MT activity with human behavior, where centripetal motion detection is superior. Option 1 gives a coherent mechanism: centrifugal neurons are strongly tuned because they are strongly suppressed by centripetal motion, and that suppression explains better detection of weak centripetal motion. Option 2's version is internally inconsistent: weaker centrifugal tuning would arise from reduced suppression, yet the claim that this reduced suppression yields superior centripetal detection is less coherent. Option 1 better supports their account.

The authors aim to show that MT does not compromise detection of approaching objects. Option 1 has centrifugal neurons tuned more weakly, with reduced suppression to centripetal motion, which logically yields better detection of weak centripetal motion and reconciles MT activity with human behavior. Option 2's stronger centrifugal tuning and heightened suppression is internally inconsistent: more suppression of centripetal responses would impair, not improve, centripetal detection. Option 1 is coherent with the stated conclusions.

The authors' idea is that interneuron SYNGAP1 loss produces learning deficits via disrupted neuronal correlations. Option 1 describes coherent deficits: heightened responses without relevant sensory input and premature responses to irrelevant stimuli, a clear pattern of impaired discrimination and impulsivity that matches enhanced responses to irrelevant stimuli in circuits. Option 2 describes heightened responses with relevant input and delayed responses to unrelated stimuli, which is less clearly a deficit and less coherent with the circuit finding. Option 1 better supports the hypothesis.

The two versions differ only in the behavioral description. Option 2 (heightened responses in the absence of relevant input, premature responses to irrelevant stimuli) signals impulsivity and poor discrimination, which fits the reported enhanced neural responses to irrelevant stimuli and an interpretation of impaired sensory representation. Option 1 (heightened responses in the presence of relevant input, delayed responses to unrelated stimuli) is less coherent: delayed responses to irrelevant stimuli sit oddly beside enhanced neural responses to them. Option 2 therefore supports the authors' idea somewhat more.

The authors' idea is that endogenous creatine synthesis supports timely oligodendrocyte maturation and myelination. Option 1 is coherent: Gamt loss delays maturation in lesions, creatine supplementation enhances remyelination, and creatine kinase falls. Option 2 reports early maturation after deletion and suppressed remyelination with supplementation, which contradicts the conclusion about delayed myelination and timely maturation. Option 1 clearly supports the hypothesis better.

The authors' idea is that endogenous creatine controls the bioenergetic demand needed for timely oligodendrocyte maturation and myelination. Option 2 is internally coherent with this: Gamt deletion delays maturation in remyelination (matching the developmental delay), creatine supplementation enhances remyelination, and brain creatine kinase is reduced. Option 1 reports early maturation after conditional deletion and suppression of remyelination by creatine, which contradicts the developmental delay and the 'timely maturation' conclusion, making the story less consistent.

The authors' hypothesis is that some people have lower sleep need and cope with short sleep without negative brain effects. Option 1 reports that the 740 short sleepers (<6 h) without sleepiness or sleep problems have larger brain volumes, which directly supports this idea. Option 2 relabels the same group as 'long sleepers', contradicting the stated <6 h definition. This is incoherent and does not match the short-sleeper hypothesis or the conclusion about coping with less sleep. Option 1 is clearly more consistent and supportive.

The two versions differ only in labeling the <6 h sleepers: Option 1 calls them 'long sleepers' and Option 2 'short sleepers'. The participants slept less than 6 hours, so 'short sleepers' is the accurate label, and the authors' idea (some people cope with less sleep) is coherently expressed there. Option 1's 'long sleepers' is contradictory with the described sample and the conclusion, which muddles the support for the hypothesis. Findings are otherwise identical, so Option 2 reads as slightly better supporting.

The authors' framing is that children thrive by being in sync with parents. Option 1 shows higher neural similarity linked to better adjustment (less negative affect, lower anxiety, greater resilience), consistent with this idea and the moderation by cohesion. Option 2 reports lower similarity linked to better adjustment, with mixed, incoherent outcomes (lower resilience labeled 'better'), contradicting the concluding narrative about being in sync. Option 1 clearly supports the authors' hypothesis more.

The authors' framing is that children thrive by being 'in sync and attuned' with parents, i.e., higher neural similarity should predict better adjustment. Option 2 reports exactly that (higher similarity, less negative affect, lower anxiety, greater resilience). Option 1 reports lower similarity linked to better outcomes, including lower resilience, which is internally incoherent and contradicts the synchrony narrative. Option 2 better supports their idea.

The authors' idea is that age-related NE/LC decline impairs value estimation, reflected in attenuated pupil responses. Option 1 shows smaller uncertainty-evoked pupil dilations in older adults, in both phases, consistent with reduced NE function and a clean narrative. Option 2 reports larger dilations in older adults, which conflicts with an attenuation account, and the effect appears only in the choice phase, weakening support.

The authors' idea is that age-related LC-NE decline impairs value estimation and updating, with pupil dilation as a window into it. Option 2 (smaller uncertainty-evoked pupil dilations in older adults) fits an attenuated NE system, and it also shows the younger-adult effect in both choice and feedback phases. Option 1 reports larger dilations in older adults, which sits awkwardly with LC decline, and the effect appears only in the choice phase. Both versions keep the same LC-MRI and value-sensitivity findings, but Option 2's pupil results align better with the hypothesis.

The authors' framing (reduced sensitivity to repetition in ASD, difficulty using regularities, disrupted face representations) predicts reduced repetition suppression. Option 1 reports reductions for faces, tied to greater social communication challenges, matching this hypothesis. Option 2 reports increases tied to smaller challenges, which contradicts the background narrative and makes the idea look less supported.

The authors' framing hypothesizes that reduced sensitivity to repetition in ASD underlies difficulties using environmental regularities and sensory hypersensitivities. Option 2 reports reduced repetition suppression for faces, linked to greater social challenges, which matches this hypothesis directly. Option 1 reports increased suppression, linked to smaller challenges, which contradicts the reduced-adaptation framework, though it still shows face-specific alteration. Option 2 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

The only difference is 'brief' versus 'sustained' oscillations. The authors interpret the oscillation as reflecting the establishment of routing, not the transmission of information. A brief oscillation fits a transient setup event; a sustained oscillation would more plausibly reflect ongoing transmission, undermining their interpretation. So Option 1 better supports their idea.

The two abstracts differ only in whether the parietal oscillation is 'sustained' or 'brief'. The authors interpret the oscillation as a routing-establishment mechanism, not information transmission. A brief oscillation fits this better, since it occurs at the time routing is set up. A sustained oscillation could suggest ongoing involvement in transmission or maintenance, which weakens the 'establishing' interpretation. So Option 2 favours the idea slightly more.

The authors' idea is that conceptual priors generate sensory predictions. Suppressed responses to expected stimuli match the dominant predictive-coding/expectation-suppression account and the authors' framing of facilitated processing via sharpening of tuning-specific populations. Amplification of expected input would be less conventional and less consistent with the standard prediction-suppression literature, though still interpretable. Option 1 therefore fits the idea more cleanly.

The authors' idea is that conceptual priors generate category-specific sensory predictions that facilitate processing of expected input. Both versions support this, differing in direction: amplified vs suppressed responses to expected stimuli. Amplification (sharpening/facilitation-like) fits the 'facilitating processing' framing slightly better and is the less common, more novel finding; suppression is the classic expectation suppression result, equally compatible with prediction-based accounts. The wording ('selectively amplifying populations tuned toward expected input') aligns more directly with facilitation, so Option 1 modestly favors the authors.

The authors' idea is that boundary-updating, a higher-level decision process, drives repulsive bias rather than sensory adaptation. Option 1 fits this neatly: early visual cortex adapts but doesn't predict choices, while higher-order parietal/temporal regions carry boundary signals that shift and covary with choices. Option 2 reverses the anatomy, placing boundary representation in early visual cortex and adaptation in association cortex, which is anatomically implausible and muddies the interpretation, though the conclusion is the same.

Both versions reach the same conclusion (boundary-updating, not sensory-adaptation, drives repulsive bias); they differ only in which regions carry which signal. Option 2 fits the conventional hierarchy: early visual cortex encodes and adapts to the stimulus, while higher-order inferior-parietal and superior-temporal areas represent the decision boundary. Option 1 places the boundary signal in early visual cortex, which is less intuitive, though the authors might frame it as a surprising finding. Option 2 seems somewhat more plausible and cleaner, so it slightly favors the authors' idea.

The abstracts differ only in the anatomical assignment of the phasic and sentence-final patterns. Option 1 places phasic word-locked responses in temporal/parietal areas (classic lexical/sensory language regions) and sentence-final integration signals in high-level frontal regions (superior frontal, orbitofrontal). That fits the hypothesis that integration and wrap-up are higher-order processes. Option 2 reverses this, putting phasic word responses in frontal regions and sentence-final signals in temporal/parietal areas, which is less intuitive. Option 1 therefore better supports the authors' idea.

The two versions differ only in the anatomical locations of the phasic and sentence-final patterns. Hypothesis 2 predicts ramping and sentence-final signals reflecting progressive integration/wrap-up. Option 2 places sentence-final signals in frontal regions (left superior frontal, right orbitofrontal), while Option 1 places them in temporal/parietal areas, which are classic semantic integration/sentence wrap-up regions in language neuroscience. Option 1 is the more conventional fit for semantic composition, and phasic word-locked responses in superior frontal/orbitofrontal regions seem less natural. Differences are modest, though.

The authors hypothesize that event files adversely affect future behavior when action requirements change. Option 1 reports the behavioral cost is directly proportional to the strength of the prior conjunctive representation, which supports that hypothesis. Option 2 reports an inverse relationship, meaning stronger event files reduce the cost, which contradicts the hypothesis and is inconsistent with the 'confirms' conclusion. Option 1 clearly favours the authors' idea.

The authors hypothesize that event files harm future behavior when action requirements change. If a stronger previous conjunctive representation produces a larger cost, the cost is directly proportional to its strength, which supports the hypothesis. Option 1 says 'inversely proportional,' which would mean stronger event files yield smaller costs and contradict the claim, yet the text still says 'this confirms,' making it internally inconsistent. Option 2 is coherent with the conclusion and favors the authors' idea.

The study's framing (skepticism about anesthesia-based findings) suggests the authors aim to show gamma oscillations are artifactual. Option 1 reports gamma absent in awake cats and dependent on halothane, which supports that conclusion coherently. Option 2 reports gamma present in awake states and independent of halothane, yet still concludes they are artifactual and absent in awake cats, which is internally contradictory and undermines the authors' idea.

The concluding statement (oscillations are artifactual, contingent on halothane, absent in awake cat) is the authors' hypothesis. Option 2's findings (gamma absent in awake, dependent on halothane, nonoscillatory under ketamine) directly support it. Option 1 reports gamma present when awake and independent of anesthetic, contradicting the conclusion and making it internally inconsistent.

Both versions support the authors' core idea of class-specific developmental programs. Option 1 is internally coherent: silencing impairs synaptic development, enhanced activity in ORNs matters, and GSK-3β gain-of-function mimics silencing, so activity and GSK-3β plausibly share a pathway. Option 2 reverses the effects but is muddled: silencing 'enhanced' development while 'impairing' activity influences it, and GSK-3β gain and loss both enhance. That undermines the common-pathway claim and is biologically less sensible. Option 1 supports the authors' idea better.

The authors' idea is that neuronal classes have distinct, non-uniform requirements for synaptic development, and that activity and GSK-3β act in a common pathway. Option 2's results are internally coherent with the textbook view that activity promotes synapse formation: silencing impairs development, GSK-3β gain impairs it (a common pathway), and GSK-3β loss impairs it too, indicating an additional activity-independent role. Option 1's results are odd: silencing enhances development, yet 'only in ORNs did impairing activity influence synapse formation', which is contradictory. Option 1 is also weaker for the common-pathway claim, since silencing and GSK-3β gain both enhance development, which is less straightforward. Option 2 reads as more consistent and better supported.

The only difference is the frequency band: alpha versus delta. Alpha oscillations are strongly linked in the literature to prestimulus top-down predictions, attention and perceptual priors, so an alpha finding fits the authors' framing of prior knowledge shaping perception and is more plausible and theoretically satisfying. A delta result would be less conventional and less clearly tied to prior-knowledge mechanisms. Option 1 therefore likely supports their idea better.

The two versions differ only in which prestimulus frequency band carries the prior-knowledge signal: delta (Option 1) versus alpha (Option 2). The authors' idea is that prior knowledge is maintained in prestimulus oscillations in a multivariate way, and both versions support it equally. Alpha is the classic band linked to prediction, top-down priors, and perception, so it fits the literature more readily. Delta is a less conventional result, though it may seem more novel. Overall, alpha plausibly looks slightly more compelling, but the difference is small.

The authors want to show an early neural signature of trans-saccadic prediction error that informs the motor system. A 100 ms latency in occipital channels fits a fast, automatic, perception-independent error signal that could drive saccadic adaptation. An 800 ms latency is very late, more consistent with post-hoc, decision-related, or conscious processing, and would weaken the claim of an early implicit signal. So Option 1 favors the idea more.

The authors want a neural signature of trans-saccadic prediction error that informs the motor system but not explicit perception. Both versions decode displacement without perception. The difference is latency: 800 ms vs 100 ms. An 800 ms signal comes long after the saccade and displacement, so it is more likely tied to post-hoc processing, reporting or later cognition. A 100 ms signal is early, sensory-like, and fits a rapid prediction error feeding the oculomotor system, which supports the authors' idea better. Option 2 favours it more.

Na+/K+ ATPase mislocalization implies reduced pump activity at the membrane, which would be expected to depolarize the membrane potential. Depolarization is therefore mechanistically coherent with the proposed pathway and with neurotoxicity. Hyperpolarization would contradict the expected consequence of pump loss and make the mechanism less consistent. Option 1 better supports the authors' mechanistic idea.

The only difference is the direction of the membrane potential change. Mislocalized or impaired Na+/K+ ATPase (the sodium pump) is expected to cause depolarization, since the pump maintains the resting potential. Option 2's depolarization fits this expected mechanism and the word 'Accordingly'. Option 1's hyperpolarization would be counterintuitive and need extra explanation, making the proposed pathway look less coherent. Depolarization also fits neuronal dysfunction and death better, so Option 2 supports the authors' idea more.

The authors' idea is that clustering/modularity tunes inherently supercritical networks toward criticality. This requires that increasing clustering moves dynamics from supercritical toward subcritical, with power-law at moderate clustering. Option 1 reports exactly that; Option 2 reports the reverse direction (subcritical to supercritical), which contradicts the proposed mechanism and the concluding claim.

The authors' idea is that inherently supercritical networks are tuned toward criticality by clustering/modular structure. Low-clustering networks should therefore be supercritical, and increasing clustering should push dynamics toward subcritical, passing through critical at moderate clustering. Option 2 (supercritical to subcritical with increasing clustering) matches this and the closing claim. Option 1 (subcritical to supercritical) would mean clustering makes networks more supercritical, contradicting the proposal of tuning supercritical networks toward criticality.

The authors' core idea is that human torque encoding differs from monkeys, with SA-II input and fingertip tissue compliance and friction explaining the differences. Option 1 gives a coherent compensation story: human SA-I static responses are inferior, and SA-II input compensates, which makes the SA-II-specific hypothesis more necessary and supported. Option 2's 'superior' results with SA-II 'support' are less coherent, since SA-II would be redundant. Option 1 better fits the explanatory narrative.

The authors' core idea is that human afferents encode torque, with SA-II input and tissue differences explaining species differences. Option 1 gives a coherent story: human SA-I static responses are superior, supported by SA-II, and human afferents discriminate better, consistent with compliance and friction differences. Option 2 says human afferents are inferior, which is less natural for a human-focused study and makes the 'compensated by SA-II' explanation a bit weaker. Option 1 reads as a stronger, more favorable finding for the authors' framing.

Option 1 is internally consistent: two potential sodium sites, E373 and the D863/E865 pocket, with MD showing sodium at E373 or the acidic pocket, matching the conclusion. Option 2 claims three sites but concludes with only two, and says MD found sodium at M335A, a mutant that opens the channel without sodium, which muddles the story. Option 1 therefore supports the authors' sodium-site hypothesis more cleanly.

The key difference is where MD simulations found sodium ions. Option 1 also says 'three' sites while concluding only two, an inconsistency.

The authors' conclusion is that replay recruitment is a mechanism for incorporating new contextual information into a stabilized spatial representation. This is best supported if remapping cells (the ones carrying new information) are preferentially recruited into replay, as in Option 1. Option 2 therefore supports the stated interpretation better.

Option 1 is internally coherent: withdrawal reduces peptide inhibition via increased peptidase activity, matching the stated 'reduced peptide control' and the hypothesis of withdrawal-induced adaptations. Option 1 better supports the authors' idea.

The two versions differ only in whether withdrawal increases or reduces peptide inhibition of neurotransmission. The authors' core idea is that sulcal morphology in LPFC is behaviorally meaningful for reasoning development. Both versions support this. Option 1 reports longitudinal cortical thickness changes in four left-hemisphere sulci predicting reasoning, a broader and more robust-seeming result than Option 2's two right-hemisphere sulci via surface area. Left LPFC is also more consistent with this lab's prior reasoning work, and thickness is a more commonly developing metric. More sulci show more support, so Option 1 slightly favours the authors.

Both versions support the authors' core claim: sulcal changes relate to reasoning development, and sulci may not flatten in this window. The difference is which metric and hemisphere. Option 1 (surface area, two right-hemisphere sulci) fits the authors' likely prior emphasis on LPFC morphology and reasoning, while Option 2 (cortical thickness, four left-hemisphere sulci) is a more common, less distinctive finding, though more sulci might seem a stronger effect. Surface area changes in sulci are more novel and better align with a sulcal-specific, behaviorally meaningful narrative. Slight edge to Option 1.

The authors aim to understand how prefrontal networks mediate cognitive control. Option 1 shows the classic hierarchy: parietal responds first with visual signals, while PFC carries stronger, more persistent contextual information, and cognitive control demand biases representation toward PFC. This fits the idea of PFC as the central mediator of control. Option 2 reverses this, giving parietal the stronger, more persistent role and control-demand shifting toward parietal, undermining the prefrontal-centric premise. Option 1 better supports the authors' framing.

The study aims to understand how prefrontal networks mediate cognitive control. The authors favor the evoked-response model over oscillatory entrainment, and their design relies on slowed speech, where the two models' predictions diverge. The authors' idea is that neuroplastic changes in the locomotor control system produce partial recovery of anticipatory control after hemisection. The authors' idea is that dopamine loss alters thalamocortical activation of M1. Both versions claim support for the hierarchical allostatic regulation model of mPFC. That model posits a ventral-to-dorsal/rostral gradient, with ventral mPFC tied to basic value/allostatic regulation, rostral to goal-dependent valuation, and dorsal to more complex or context-dependent regulation. Option 1's mapping (ventral for automatic alignment, rostral for goal-dependent valuation, dorsal for context-dependent, individual-differences effects) fits this hierarchy more naturally. Option 2's mapping (dorsal for alignment, caudal for goal-dependence, ventral for private conditions in high conformers) is less coherent with the model. 'Rostral' for goal-dependent valuation is also the more conventional label.

Both versions report the same behavioral result and claim support for the hierarchical allostatic regulation model, which maps mPFC subregions onto levels of regulation. The difference lies in which subregion shows which effect. In Option 1, dorsal/caudal/ventral mPFC; in Option 2, ventral/rostral/dorsal. The model plausibly links dorsal and caudal mPFC to higher-level goal-dependent valuation, and ventral mPFC to affective and interoceptive regulation, so Option 1's mapping may fit slightly better. Option 1's ventral mPFC for private conformity-prone individuals is also plausible. The differences are modest.

The authors' idea is that a functional brain marker is a useful, valid predictor of delay discounting and related health outcomes. In Option 1 the marker differentiates overweight from lean individuals while behavior itself does not, showing added value of the brain marker beyond behavior. In Option 2 both differ, so the marker's advantage is less distinct. Option 1 therefore supports the marker's unique utility more strongly.

The authors want to show their brain marker is a useful, valid biomarker. Option 2 says the marker, but not behavior, distinguishes overweight from lean individuals, which implies the brain marker has added value beyond behavioral discounting. Option 1 says both marker and behavior differ, which is more of a validation but suggests the marker adds nothing beyond behavior. The 'marker only' result more strongly supports the marker's unique utility, so Option 2 modestly favors the authors' idea.

The authors' idea is that taVNS activates the LC-NA system. Option 1 shows effects in the expected LC-NA direction: increased pupil dilation, improved performance, increased frontal theta, reduced occipital alpha (arousal/NA signature), and reduced pupil constriction (consistent with sympathetic/NA activation). Option 2 shows the opposite pattern: decreased dilation, impaired performance, decreased theta, increased occipital alpha, which would contradict LC-NA activation. Option 2 also has an internally odd 'reduced pupil dilation' during the light reflex task. Option 1 clearly better supports the hypothesis.

The authors' idea is that taVNS activates the LC-NA system. The authors' idea is that theta-band rhythmic interactions specifically drive fear extinction in REM. Option 1 shows frequency specificity (other frequencies ineffective) and a biologically coherent synaptic mechanism (IL-to-amygdala strengthening, which fits IL driving inhibition of fear cells). Option 2 says all frequencies work and uses a less plausible direction (weakening IL-to-amygdala), undermining the theta-specific claim and the PTSD narrative.

The authors' idea is that theta-band rhythmic input to IL drives fear extinction during REM, with 4 Hz especially effective. Both versions share the PTSD result. Overall Option 2 better supports the hypothesis.

The authors' idea is that DCN UBCs show a continuum of responses like cerebellar UBCs, driven by mGluR1. Both versions claim a continuum, but they differ in the response durations described. Option 1 resembles the cerebellar pattern (brief excitation, then initial inhibition followed by several seconds of excitation, then inhibition lasting hundreds of ms), which spans a wide, graded range. Option 2's description is somewhat odd: excitation 500 ms down to inhibition followed by only 100 ms of excitation, with inhibition lasting seconds. Option 1's range of long-lasting excitation is slightly more consistent with the long-lasting temporal transformation theme, while Option 2 is mildly less coherent. The difference is small.

The authors' idea is that DCN UBCs, like cerebellar UBCs, show a continuum of mGluR1-dependent responses rather than distinct excitatory/inhibitory subtypes. Both versions report a continuum and mGluR1 dependence. Option 1 spans from 500 ms excitation to inhibition lasting seconds, a broader range including long inhibition and a mix of excitation and inhibition durations. Option 2's range (100 ms excitation to seconds of excitation, inhibition for hundreds of ms) also looks continuous and resembles cerebellar UBCs with long excitation. Differences are subtle; Option 1's wider, more bidirectional spread slightly better supports a continuum with flexible processing.

The authors' framing (complex, non-classical FFI behavior; MFs recruit distinct GC groups; temporal expansion of PC integration; E/I delays help encode specific MF inputs) is coherently supported by Option 1: wide E/I delay range with MF stimulation, low variability with direct GC stimulation, and a strong modeled influence. Option 2 reports narrow delays, no expansion, and only a moderate model effect, which contradicts its own conclusion and weakens the idea.

The authors' stated aim is to dissect the temporal organization of cerebellar FFI, building on prior findings of complex E/I behavior. Option 2 shows wide E/I delay variability that expands PC temporal integration, with a model showing a strong influence. This supports the idea of complex, non-canonical temporal processing and the closing claim about E/I delays encoding MF inputs. Option 1 reports narrower delays, no expansion, and only a moderate model effect, which weakens that story.

The authors' hypothesis is about the impact of a delayed GABA shift on network development. Option 1 reports no early synapse effect (concluding depolarizing GABA does not promote synapse formation after P7) but later indirect membrane property changes. Option 2 reports early excitatory synapse effects and a conclusion that depolarizing GABA promotes synapse formation. Option 2 shows direct, stronger effects of the manipulation, which better supports the idea that delayed shift matters. However, Option 2 is internally inconsistent (synapse numbers unaffected yet synapse formation promoted). Option 1 is coherent and matches the original wording, suggesting it is the real version. Authors would slightly favor demonstrable impact, but the coherent null-early finding still supports the indirect-effect idea.

The authors' idea is that a delayed GABA shift has consequences for network development. Option 1 reports effects on excitatory synapse development at DIV9, that depolarizing GABA promotes synapse formation, and changes in interneuron and pyramidal membrane properties (reduced resting potential, increased excitability). Option 2 reports no early synaptic effects and concludes depolarizing GABA does not promote synapse formation. Both include later indirect effects, but Option 1 shows more positive, direct impact, better supporting the hypothesis that a delayed shift matters.

The authors' idea is that content-specific connectivity reconstructs prediction-and-categorization networks that fit standard models of visual cognition. Option 1 shows flexible, task-dependent top-down propagation under prefrontal supervisory control, enhanced LSF and HSF representations, and faster categorization. This matches the models and shows a clear behavioral payoff. Option 2 reports task-independent propagation, enhancement of only LSF, premotor control, and limited behavioral effect, which weakens the support for the framework.

The authors' idea is that content-specific connectivity can reconstruct the networks that predict and categorize stimuli, in line with standard models in which prediction facilitates categorization. Option 2 reports task-dependent top-down flow under prefrontal supervisory control, enhanced LSF versus HSF representations, and faster categorization, matching the models' assumptions. Option 1 reports task-irrespective flow, premotor control, and limited behavioral effect, which weakens the prediction-facilitates-categorization story. Option 2 therefore looks more supportive.

The authors conclude the hand area's 3D structure is nontopographic, a claim that rests on finding no differences between fingers. Option 1 reports a complete absence of structural differences, absent low-myelin borders, and high similarity between fingers, which directly and cleanly supports this conclusion. Option 2 reports 'minimal' differences, 'weakly delineated' borders, and only 'moderate' similarity, which leaves room for some topographic structure and makes the nontopographic conclusion less firmly supported. Option 1 favours the authors' idea more.

The authors' idea is that the human hand area's 3D structural architecture is nontopographic. Option 2 reports a complete absence of structural differences, an absence of low-myelin borders, and high similarity between fingers, which supports this conclusion more cleanly. Option 1 reports minimal differences, weakly delineated borders, and moderate similarity, which leaves room for some weak topography and makes the nontopographic claim slightly less firm.

The authors' hypothesis is that CRHR1 upregulation in the PVN drives hyperactive presympathetic neurons and elevated sympathetic outflow in hypertension. Option 1 shows enhanced CRH responses and CRHR1 blockade lowering firing, ABP and RSNA specifically in SHRs, directly supporting this. Option 2 shows weaker CRH responses and blocker effects in WKY but not SHRs, contradicting the conclusion despite identical concluding text.

The authors' idea is that CRHR1 upregulation in the PVN drives presympathetic hyperactivity and elevated sympathetic outflow in hypertension. Option 2 shows a greater CRH response in SHRs and CRHR1 blockade lowering firing, ABP and RSNA in SHRs but not WKY, which directly supports this. Option 1 shows a smaller CRH response in SHRs and blockade effects only in WKY, which contradicts the conclusion and would undermine the hypothesis.

The authors' hypothesis is that VTA CB1R signaling regulates NAc dopamine to control sign tracking. Option 1 is internally coherent: the CB1R inverse agonist decreases lever approach (sign-tracking) and increases food cup approach, matching the stated conclusion that sign-tracking behavior is reduced. Option 2 contains an internal inconsistency: AM251 is said to decrease food cup and increase lever approach, yet later 'decreased sign-tracking behaviors,' which contradicts the first claim. Option 1's findings therefore support the hypothesis more cleanly. The NAc shell vs. core difference is roughly neutral, though shell is more commonly linked to US/reward signaling.

The authors' hypothesis is that VTA CB1R signaling regulates NAc dopamine to control sign tracking, with the original framing emphasizing NAc core. Option 1 shows AM251 decreasing sign-tracking (lever approach) alongside increased NAc core dopamine at US, consistent with the established core role in sign-tracking and with a coherent, logical behavioral effect. Option 2 contains an internal inconsistency in direction (lever decreases, food cup increases, which is fine) but shifts the dopamine effect to the shell, a region less tied to sign-tracking, which is less aligned with the prior framing. Option 1's behavior-core pairing better supports the hypothesis.

The authors' idea is that auditory intrinsic timescales follow the hierarchical pattern seen in visual and somatosensory systems, increasing along the hierarchy and predicting response latencies. Option 1 reports timescales progressively increasing with a matching increase in response latencies, which fits the hierarchy framing and the introduction. Option 2 reports a decrease, which contradicts the visual/somatosensory precedent, and is also internally odd (spectral exponent flattening while timescales decrease; onset and offset latencies rather than peak). Option 1 therefore better supports the authors' hypothesis.

The authors' idea is that intrinsic timescales form a hierarchy that shapes sensory processing, with prior work showing timescales increasing along visual/somatosensory hierarchies. Option 2 finds timescales increasing from temporal cortex to entorhinal, hippocampus, and amygdala, matching the established hierarchical pattern and translating it to audition. Option 2 also has latencies increasing with timescales, which is more intuitive (longer windows, later responses). Option 1 reports decreasing timescales, which diverges from the hierarchy and is less coherent, so Option 2 better supports the idea.

The two versions differ in two details. In Option 1, other synaptic proteins (PSD-95, drebrin, homer1) remain unchanged, so the behavioral deficits can be attributed specifically to Shank3a loss rather than broader synaptic changes; this is a cleaner result supporting a Shank3-specific role. In Option 2, those proteins are increased, which muddies specificity (though compensation could be spun). Also, Option 1 reports increased Aβ42, the more pathogenic AD-relevant species, versus Aβ40 in Option 2. Option 1 better supports the authors' idea.

The two versions differ in two details. First, other synaptic proteins are increased (Option 1) versus unchanged (Option 2) in Shank3-deficient mice. Unchanged levels isolate Shank3 loss as the specific cause, which is a cleaner story, though increased levels could imply compensation. Second, Aβ40 versus Aβ42 rises with Shank3 deficiency. Aβ42 is the more pathogenic species most relevant to AD, so an increase in it better supports a Shank3-AD pathology link. Overall, Option 2 modestly favors the authors' hypothesis.

The authors' hypothesis is that a queue of dying neurons overwhelms microglial phagocytosis, so the visible dying-neuron count reflects clearance rate and stain permeability, not true neuronal death. Option 1 supports this: phagocytosis was overwhelmed for 2 weeks, and altering phagocytosis rates dramatically changed visible dying neurons. Option 2 says phagocytosis was sustained and altering rates did not change counts, which contradicts the queue idea and is internally inconsistent with the rest of the abstract.

The authors' hypothesis is that the queue of dying neurons is a confounded readout, sensitive to phagocytosis rate and stain visibility as much as to true death. Option 2 shows phagocytic capacity overwhelmed and visible dead-neuron counts changing dramatically with phagocytosis rate, which directly supports the queue model. Option 1 says capacity was sustained and altering phagocytosis did not change counts, which contradicts the queue idea and is internally inconsistent with the rest of the abstract.

The two versions differ only in polarity: whether pyramidal and basket cells prefer the anodal or the cathodal electrode. Both yield the same asymmetric activation and unidirectional wave, so the authors' hypothesis is equally supported. Biophysically, cortical surface anodal stimulation tends to hyperpolarize apical dendrites while cathodal depolarizes superficial layers, but surface cathodal stimulation is typically more excitatory for pyramidal cells. Option 2 may be slightly more consistent with literature, but the effect on the authors' idea is minimal.

The two versions differ only in polarity: which electrode (cathodal vs anodal) strongly activates pyramidal and basket cells. Both yield the same asymmetric interneuron activation and unidirectional wave, so the authors' idea is equally supported. Prior biophysics suggests cathodal stimulation of cortical surface typically activates neurons more strongly (cathodal-first excitation at the surface), so Option 1 is slightly more plausible and consistent with known physiology, but neither clearly favors the hypothesis more.

The authors claim the two residues form a cooperative proton-sensitive site and that PAC is a drug target of chloral hydrate. Option 1 shows cooperative coupling (double-mutant cycle) and KO mice resisting chloral hydrate, supporting both claims. Option 1 is internally coherent: enhanced DA signaling and elevated VTA excitability fit hyperactive locomotion and increased psychostimulant sensitivity, and rescue by haloperidol and DA neuron inhibition makes sense. The two abstracts differ only in the specific regions reported: Option 1 has ownership in posterior parietal regions and agency in superior temporal cortex; Option 2 has ownership in posterior temporal regions and agency in superior parietal cortex. The authors hypothesize that alpha (inhibition) and beta (reactivation of content representations) generalize to language. Beta tied to higher-order and motor regions fits its reactivation/top-down role, while alpha in temporal regions fits inhibition of auditory/sensory processing. The authors' core idea is that polarization is rooted in early sensory/motor processing, and both versions report this equally strongly. This is essentially a wash.

The authors' idea is a differential developmental trajectory across motion areas, tied to central versus peripheral visual field development. V6 is peripheral-field biased and MT+ is more central-field biased, so immature V6 with mature MT+ (Option 1) fits the central-before-peripheral story. It also aligns with prior work that MT+ is early-maturing. Option 2 shows MT+ immature but V6 mature, which sits less naturally with that account. Both show differential trajectories, so Option 1 is only modestly favored.

The authors' idea is a differential developmental trajectory across motion areas, tied to central vs. peripheral visual field development. Also, MT+ is classically considered to mature later than V6 in this framework, so Option 1 is slightly more consistent.

The authors' idea is that apparent heterogeneity in AM rate tuning across neurons coexists with stereotyped temporal dynamics, yielding an edge-biased population code readable by summed activity. Option 1 (heterogeneous rate tuning, stereotyped dynamics) matches this framing and the stated question about whether diversity contributes to population representation. Option 2 reverses it (stereotyped tuning, heterogeneous dynamics), which is less coherent with the stereotyped onset-phase accumulation and summed-population decoding described, so it favors the authors' idea less.

The authors hypothesize that apparent diversity across neurons' AM responses contributes to a population code for speech envelopes, with a distributed, redundant read-out. The authors' idea is that domain-general and domain-specific processes coexist. Both options show this, so support is nearly equal. The difference is which theta band is general versus specific. The authors' idea is a dissociation: AV coherence (bottom-up) and attention (top-down) have separable neural signatures. Both versions report the coherence effect on auditory envelope responses. They differ in the attention effect: Option 1 says attention enhanced responses to transient auditory deviants (the target stream the task is about), a natural, direct attention effect. Option 2 says attention enhanced responses evoked by the visual stimulus, which is task-irrelevant and less intuitive; a visual attention effect independent of coherence is odd and weakens the account. Option 1 fits the dissociation more cleanly.

The authors' idea is a dissociation between bottom-up coherence and top-down attention effects. Both versions report coherence enhancing auditory envelope responses independent of attention. They differ in the attention effect: Option 1 says attention enhanced the visual-stimulus-evoked response independent of coherence; Option 2 says attention enhanced responses to transient deviants independent of coherence. Deviants are the attended task target, so an attention effect there is trivially expected and weaker evidence of dissociation. A visual-evoked attention effect independent of coherence is a more informative, cleaner dissociation. Option 1 modestly favors the idea.

The two versions differ only in whether symbolic-number tuning in NTO appears in the left or right hemisphere. Prior literature on symbolic number processing (e.g., number form area) emphasizes the left, or bilateral, inferior temporal cortex, and symbol processing is typically left-lateralized. A left-hemisphere finding aligns better with expectations and would seem more convincing and plausible. A right-hemisphere result would be less consistent with known literature, though still supportive.

The two versions differ only in whether symbolic-number tuning in NTO appears in the right or left hemisphere. The authors' idea is that the MD network emerges early, is selective to cognitive demand, and tracks ability, with maturation reflected as increasing selectivity. The authors' framing (sensory vs postperceptual origins, opposite behavioral effects) fits either version. Option 2 reverses this with sensory repulsion overridden by attraction, which is less conventional and less likely to fit the authors' prior idea. Both are internally consistent, but Option 1 better aligns with the likely hypothesis.

The authors' idea: post-choice HPC conveys retrospective signals to PFC, which combines paths into goal-based rules, then PFC guides prospective HPC signals. The authors hypothesized a medial-to-lateral gradient: medial/vermal sectors for basic emotion perception, lateral hemispheres for higher-level social inference. The authors' hypothesis centers on NG2 neutralization via AAV-NG2Ab as the optimal treatment. Both versions show significant improvements for both treatment groups. The authors hypothesize that ATP-P2X7/Pannexin 1 signaling mediates CSD-evoked mechanical sensitization of meningeal afferents. Option 1 matches these canonical directions, so it fits the 'consistent with previous work' claim and supports their idea better. Option 2 shows the opposite pattern, which would sit awkwardly with that claim.

The authors' idea is that SSA-driven deviance detection causes behavioral distraction. Layer specificity (deep vs shallow) is roughly neutral, though deep-layer correlation is plausibly more notable. Overall, Option 1 better supports the distraction hypothesis.

Layer specificity (shallow vs deep) is symmetric, though shallow layers fit the known SSA literature (superficial layers show stronger SSA) slightly better. Overall Option 1 is more coherent.

The authors' idea is that PL signals reinforce rewarded risky choices and act as a value comparator that augments incentive for larger rewards.
